Characteristic features: similar to the Black Morel (Morchella conica), differing in its rounder, irregularly and more deeply honeycombed cap. Grows singly or in small groups, likes humus-rich soil. A valuable edible mushroom. Common, more widespread than the Black Morel.

valgomasis-nuosedis.features: Massive, purplish-bluish-brown fruiting bodies, spores large
desc: Fruiting bodies large. Cap 10-15 (20) cm across, slimy, when grown matt, fleshy, dark brownish-greyish-violet, violet-chestnut, purplish-bluish-brown, chocolate-brown. Young gills violet, greyish, eventually reddish-brown, dark, adnate. Stem 5-15 (20) x 1.5-3 cm, thickening towards the base, swollen at the base, thickened to 5 cm across and more, bluish-violet, with fibres of the bluish veil, woolly, when old greyish, fibrous. Flesh whitish, in the stem bluish, firm, with a pleasant smell and taste. Characteristic features: cap, gills and stem with a violet tinge; grows under oaks and hazels. Appears singly or in small groups in deciduous, rarely coniferous forests. Warmth-loving.

valgomasis-pievagrybis.habitat: Meadows, pastures, gardens, parks, forest edges, fields, fallow land
valgomasis-pievagrybis.features: Fruiting bodies white, turning brownish. Stem with a ring, without a volva
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized, rarely large. Cap 5-10 (12) cm across, convex-flattened, finely fibrous, scaly, fleshy, white, later whitish, brownish-white. Gills whitish-pink, pinkish-brown, blackish-brown. Stem 5—8x1—2.5 cm, white, round, hollow, with a white, downward-hanging ring. Flesh fleshy, white, turning slightly brownish when broken, with a pleasant smell and taste. Characteristic features: similar to the Horse Mushroom, only the fruiting bodies are smaller, turn yellowish when pressed, the flesh turns slightly reddish when cut, and it is more aromatic. Grows in groups or singly, likes fertile soil, cultivated artificially. A valuable edible mushroom. Common.

Small mushrooms. Cap 1-2 cm across, rarely larger (3-4 cm), round, matt, sometimes wrinkled, thin, greyish-brown, pinkish-brown, leather-brown. Gills grey, narrow, crowded, adnate. Stem long, about 10 cm above ground and 3-7 cm in the soil, in the litter, on a cone or growing through it. Characteristic features: very tough, appears very early in spring, as soon as the snow has melted. Grows singly. Small, but pleasant in taste, good for flavouring soups. A mushroom highly valued by the Germans. A harbinger of spring. Very similar is Strobilurus stephanocystis (S. stephanocystis), which grows at the same time but on pine cones. Edible, common.

valgomoji-geltonpinte.habitat: On willows, oaks and other trees
desc: Fruiting bodies fleshy, annual, large, up to 1 m across, several layers of flat, semicircular, fan- or spatula-shaped caps fused like roof tiles, attached to the substrate by a broad, thickened edge. The cap surface is wrinkled, orange, yellowish-orange in colour. Tubes up to 4 pm long, sulphur-yellow. Flesh up to 3 cm thick, soft, juicy, fleshy, yellowish, slightly sour in taste. Characteristic features: grows on deciduous, very rarely coniferous trees as a biotroph or as a saprotroph (in forests, parks, squares). Grows on injured parts of tree trunks, at various heights, rarely higher than 3 m. Causes a rapidly spreading heart rot. Edible when young. Very common. Of interest to medical scientists.

valgomoji-voveraite.season: Summer, autumn, sometimes also in May
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 3-10 (15) cm across, yellow, fading. There are no gills; there are thick, crimped, branched, gill-like veins, the colour of the cap. Stem tapered. Tasty, one of the favourite mushrooms of mushroom pickers. Grows slowly, is almost never maggoty, and even once grown it lasts 2-3 weeks or even a month and more without spoiling. Easy to transport, very valuable commercially. Its nutritional value is debatable, as it contains a lot of indigestible matter - chitin, but it is highly valued by cooks; moreover, the chanterelle is also of interest to medical scientists. Mushroom pickers should not tear up the forest litter and mosses when searching for tiny chanterelles: this harms not only them but also other mushrooms and the forest.

Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap bluntly conical, rarely globular, 3-5x2-3 cm in size, from pale to dark grey or even greyish-brown in colour; the alveoli labyrinth-like, polygonal, round or irregular in shape. Stem 2-8x1-2 cm, thickening towards the base, white, yellowish. Flesh greyish, brittle, with a pleasant smell and taste. Characteristic features: differs from the Common Morel in its conical cap shape, grey colour and larger alveoli. Grows singly or in small groups, on soil. A tasty edible mushroom. Rare.

variaspalve-geltonpede.features: Cap dry, smooth, shiny, stem the colour of the cap, tapering
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 3—5 cm, less often 8—12 cm across. Conical, dry, copper-coloured, orange-yellowish-brownish, shiny. Gills pale brown. Stem 5-10x1-2.5 cm in size, almost the colour of the cap, with remnants of a ring near the gills. Flesh orange, with a pleasant smell and taste. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies copper-coloured. Grows singly or a few fruiting bodies together in coniferous forests, most often in dry, old pine forests. Edible, does not blacken when boiled. Common.

variaspalvis-nuosedis.features: Stem not bulbous at the base, bluish when young, spores large
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 5-8 (10) cm across, flattened-convex, horizontal, slimy, yellowish-brown, reddish-brown, the margins paler. Young gills bluish, when mature reddish-brown, sinuate. Stem 5-10x1-3 cm, thickening evenly towards the base, white, fibrous, with a bluish tinge, when old yellowish-brown, with a ring-like remnant of the brown veil. Flesh whitish, with a mild smell and taste, thick. Characteristic features: cap brown; the gills are violet-bluish until the spores mature. Grows singly or in small groups in spruce and pine forests, likes calcareous soil. Edible.

Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 3-7 (10) cm across, bell-shaped, later irregularly flattened, with a blunt umbo in the middle, smooth, finely fibrous, dark greyish-brown, blackish-brown, yellowish-greyish-brown. Gills thin, crowded, whitish, grey, adnate. Stem 3-10x0.3-1.3 cm, slightly thickening towards the base, whitish, grey, when old greyish-brownish. Flesh thin, tough, with a mealy, woody smell and a slightly bitter taste. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies tough, cap depressed, slightly bitter in taste. Grows in larger or smaller groups, sometimes in clumps, rarely singly, in grassy places, likes humus-rich soil. Edible. Very common.

velyvoji-tauriabude.features: Cap greyish-ochre, depressed, margins bent downwards
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 2-4 (5) cm across, convex-flattened, shallowly depressed, dark yellowish-grey, greyish-yellowish, pale ochre, fading to greyish, the margins translucent, grooved. Gills white, greyish-yellowish, crowded, narrow, decurrent or broadly adnate. Stem 2-4x0.3-0.5 cm, the colour of the cap, with white hairs at the base, firmly attached to the substrate. Flesh cream-coloured, thin, with a faint mealy smell, not bitter. Characteristic features: grows in autumn and early spring, in pine and spruce forests. Appears singly or in small groups. Edible, of low value. Uncommon.

violetinis-nuosedis.features: Fruiting bodies with a cedar smell, spores large
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized, large. Cap 5-10 (12) cm across, sometimes larger, bell-shaped, later convex-flattened, fleshy, the surface rough, fibrous, felty, even scaly; when young bluish-violet, later brownish, brownish-violet. Young gills dark violet, when mature bluish-brown, adnate. Stem 7-10x1—2 cm, violet-brown, the base club-shaped, thickened. Flesh with violet streaks, thick, with a delicate smell of cedar and juniper wood. Characteristic features: cap, stem, gills and flesh violet-blue; cap surface rough, felty. Grows singly or a few fruiting bodies together. Edible. Should be assigned to the protected species.

voveraitine-guotele.habitat: Deciduous, coniferous and mixed forests, sandy places
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized, most often small. Cap 3-5 (8) cm across, fleshy, orange, orange-red, fading to yellow or even yellowish, velvety. Gills narrow, forked, orange-red, decurrent. Stem the colour of the cap, tapering, 3-5x0.5—1 (1.5) cm in size. Flesh yellowish, orange, without a particular smell or taste. Characteristic features: very similar to the Chanterelle, only less fleshy, more delicate, of a brighter orange colour, and sometimes growing even on rotten wood. Likes rotten pine and spruce stumps, their debris, or the sandy roots of fallen spruces or pines. Very common, edible, but of low value; collecting it for food is not recommended.

vysninis-miltagrybis.habitat: Deciduous and coniferous forests, mossy places
vysninis-miltagrybis.features: Fruiting bodies white, gills decurrent, with a pink tinge
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized (small). Cap 3-8 cm across, rarely grows larger, when young white, later greyish-white, matt, fibrous, fleshy. Gills white, when old with a pink tinge, decurrent. Stem 2-6x0.3-1.3 cm, white, central, sometimes eccentric, tapering downwards. Flesh white, soft, with a strong mealy smell, not bitter. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies of the funnel (Clitocybe) or domecap (Lyophyllum) type, but whitish, greyish in colour, soft, with a mealy smell. Grows singly, most often a few fruiting bodies together. Edible, but of low value. Fairly common.

zaliuoke.habitat: Coniferous (especially pine forests), rarely deciduous forests
zaliuoke.features: Cap, gills and stem yellow, sulphur-coloured, also grows late in autumn
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized, rarely large. Cap 3-7 (12) cm across, convex-flattened, when old horizontal, with an umbo, fibrous, scaly, greenish-yellow, yellowish-greenish, greenish-brown, slimy, dry in dry weather, covered with sand. Gills greenish-yellow, yellow, adnate, free. Stem 2-6x1-3 cm, of uniform thickness, usually the colour of the gills. Flesh thick, firm, juicy, whitish, yellowish, with a pleasant smell and taste. Characteristic features: mostly a mushroom of dry pine forests. Grows in groups. Edible, a mushroom much loved and eaten by everyone. In 2004 the press wrote about the Yellow Knight as a poisonous mushroom, but this is unbelievable and incomprehensible. Nothing has been heard of poisonings by the Yellow Knight in Lithuania.

Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 3—10 cm across, velvety, yellowish-brown, greenish-yellowish-brown, greenish-brown, usually with a yellowish tinge. Stem 5—10 cm long and 1-2.5 cm thick, yellowish, yellowish-brownish, greyish-yellowish. Flesh white, soft, slightly turning blue or pinkish. Characteristic features: stem thin, of uneven thickness, without a red bloom. Grows singly or in small groups. Common. Eaten fresh, pickled, dried. The Suede Bolete and the Red Cracking Bolete are heavily attacked by the golden bolete mould (Hypomyces chrysospermus Bull.). In some places this mushroom is also called šilbaravykis (pine-heath bolete).

zalsvoji-umede.features: Fruiting bodies more robust than those of the Green Brittlegill, cap firm, cracked
desc: Fruiting bodies large. Cap 5-10 (13-15) cm across, convex-flattened, sometimes depressed, margins bent downwards, fleshy, firm, greenish, greyish-yellowish-greenish, the cuticle cracked, fissured. Young gills white, later pale cream, brownish, adnexed. Stem 3 -8 (10)x 1.5-4 (5) cm, firm, brittle, white, when old becoming greyish, spotted brownish. Flesh up to 2 cm thick, white, firm, with a pleasant smell and taste. Characteristic features: cap massive, greenish, the margins paler; warmth-loving. Grows singly or in small groups, likes the company of oak and birch and calcareous soil. Rare. Edible, valuable. Should be classed as protected. When collecting green, greenish brittlegills, be very careful: the Death Cap may grow nearby, and it will mercilessly punish anyone who makes a mistake.

zieduotasis-nuosedis.habitat: Damp mixed forests, especially under birches
zieduotasis-nuosedis.features: Cap reddish-brown, fibrous, gills yellowish-brown, toothed
desc: Fruiting bodies large. Cap 5-10 (12-15) cm across, matt, radially fibrous, reddish-yellowish-brown, brick-red. Gills yellowish-brownish, brown, the edges notched, adnate. Stem 5-10 (12-15)x 1-1.5 cm, white, later pinkish, greyish-brown, with 2-3 or even 5 ring-like remnants of the red veil, usually encircling the stem obliquely. Flesh yellowish, without a particular smell, not bitter. Characteristic features: brownish stem with 2-3 (5) ring-like bands of the red veil. Grows in small groups in coniferous and mixed forests. A webcap easily recognised by the multiple red bands on its stem. Edible. Of low value.

zvynuotasis-nuosedis.features: Young gills violet, old ones brown
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized, large. Cap 5-10 (12) cm across, when young conical, when old flattened, usually with a blunt umbo, densely covered with brown fibrous scales on a yellowish background. Veil violet. Gills pale violet, quickly becoming pale brown, brown, adnexed. Stem 5-12 (14) x1-2 cm, with a ring-like remnant, violet above it, below it, like the cap, brown-fibrous, scaly. Flesh brownish, without a particular smell or taste. Characteristic features: cap and stem brown-fibrous, scaly. Grows singly or in small groups in forests, most often under birches and aspens, in damp grassy places. Common, edible. An easily recognised webcap.

zvynuotoji-baravykpinte.habitat: In coniferous forests, especially sandy pine forests
zvynuotoji-baravykpinte.features: Tubes very short, flesh turns pink when broken and darkens
desc: Fruiting bodies large. Cap 5-15 cm across, fleshy, irregularly shaped, the surface smooth, matt, greyish-brown, blackish-grey, in old mushrooms cracked, as if finely scaly. Tubes white, greyish, short. Stem 2-5 (8)x-3 cm, central or eccentric, the colour of the cap. Flesh white, stained violet-pink when cut, later darkening to blackish. Characteristic features: dirty greyish-blackish-brownish, firm fruiting bodies. Grows singly. Edible, but of no special taste. Rare. Protected.

zvynuotoji-skujagalve.features: Cap and stem very scaly, not slimy
desc: Fruiting bodies large. Cap 5-10 (15) cm across, yellowish-brownish, ochre-brownish, densely covered with sharp brown scales. Young gills greenish-yellow, old ones reddish-brown, adnate. Stem 7-15x0.5-1.5 (3) cm, like the cap, conspicuously yellowish-brown-scaly. Flesh greenish-yellowish, tough, not bitter, with an unpleasant smell. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies brownish-yellow, fibrous-scaly, shaggy, growing in colonies. Appears on snags, windfalls, stumps, at the bases of living trees, in injured places, in large groups. Edible, but of low value. Common.

zvynuotoji-skyletbude.habitat: On stumps and windfalls of deciduous trees
zvynuotoji-skyletbude.features: Cap irregularly shaped, large, scaly, spores large
desc: An annual mushroom. Cap 5—30 (60) across, 2—6 cm thick, irregularly shaped, yellowish, covered with dark brown, radially arranged scales. Tubes up to 7 mm long, yellowish, brownish. Stem 3-10x3-5 cm, woody, lateral, yellowish, black at the base. Flesh up to 4 cm thick, corky, with a woody smell, yellowish.
Characteristic features: fruiting bodies very large; the mushroom is fairly common, especially on stumps in parks and along roadsides. Edible when young.

agurkine-didpusle.habitat: Meadows, shores, ditch sides, forests, among grasses
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 2-5 cm across, when young conical, later bell-shaped, eventually convex-flattened, with an umbo, hygrophanous, matt, chestnut, dark brown, fading, the margins paler, barely grooved. Gills crowded, narrow, greyish, later pinkish-yellowish, adnate. Stem 3-7x0.3-0.7 cm, straight, tapering towards the base, slightly velvety, brownish-black, paler near the gills. Flesh thin, tough, not bitter, with a smell of cucumber or fish. Cystidia large, pointed, 55-90x15-20 pm. Characteristic features: cap chestnut, stem velvety, black in colour, with a strong smell of cucumber. Grows singly or in small groups, on the ground, among grasses.

aitrusis-pusynbaravykis.habitat: Coniferous forests, most often close to pine trunks
aitrusis-pusynbaravykis.features: Tubes and pores pink, bitter taste
desc: Fruiting bodies large. Cap 5-15 cm across, fleshy, matt, not shiny, brown with a yellow or grey tinge. Tubes 1.5–2.5 cm long, white, later pink, pores very fine, turning brown when pressed. Stem 6-12x1-5 cm, thickening towards the base, only near the cap with a net of white elongated meshes, yellowish-brownish. Flesh white, not changing colour, firm, later brownish, bitter. Characteristic features: underside of the cap pink, flesh bitter, very similar to the porcini.
Grows singly and in small groups in spruce and pine forests. Very common. Inedible: after boiling several times it loses its bitterness, but is still not suitable for eating.

alksnynine-raistabude.habitat: Damp, grassy black-alder woods, forests, bogs, shrublands
alksnynine-raistabude.features: Cap furrowed, stem without a ring, spores large, granular
desc: Fruiting bodies tiny. Cap 1-2 cm across, broadly bell-shaped when young, flattened when mature, with a slight umbo and sometimes even depressed, fragile, translucent, furrowed, dark reddish-brown, fading to yellowish ochre. Gills whitish ochre, reddish-brown, edges finely white-toothed, notched. Stem 3-5 (6)x0.1–0.3 cm, fragile, cream-coloured, reddish-brown when old, lower part blackish-brown, fibrous. Flesh very thin, brown, with a smell of stale flour and a slightly bitter taste. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies reddish-brown, fading, appearing only under alders. Grows in small groups. Inedible. Very common. Saprotroph.

amiantine-slakabude.features: Cap granular, stem the colour of the cap, fibrous
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 2-3 cm across, flattened, with an umbo, finely fibrous-granular, the margin with white, yellowish remnants of the partial veil, from pale to ochre-yellow, orange, fading to yellowish. Gills white, narrow, crowded, yellowish when old, adnate. Stem 4-8x0.3-0.3 cm, with an inconspicuous ring, above which it is smooth, finely dotted, below it granular and fibrous like the cap. Flesh thin, yellowish, brownish-yellow, with an unpleasant smell and taste. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies fibrous, yellowish-ochre, spores amyloid. Grows singly or in small groups among mosses. Inedible. Very common, much more common than the granular or cinnabar powdercap.

Fruiting bodies small. Cap 3–5 cm across, convex, flattened, with an umbo, sometimes depressed, reddish yellow-brown, greenish-brown. Young gills cream, old ones greyish-brown, chocolate, adnate. Stem 3-4x0.2-0.5 cm, elastic, tough, pale yellowish, fibrous. Flesh thin, yellowish, not bitter, smelling of wood. Characteristic features: grows only on burnt ground and bonfire sites, which is unusual for most agaricoid fungi, especially for brittlestems, scalycaps and stumpcaps. Grows in larger or smaller groups on old fire sites. Inedible. Very common. After fires have devastated forests, it is one of the first to start growing in these places; foresters should make use of this property when replanting forests.

anglinis-tauriukas.habitat: Old burnt areas and bonfire sites, forests, parks
anglinis-tauriukas.features: Fruiting bodies trumpet- or horn-shaped, yellowish-brown
desc: Fruiting bodies tiny, 1-2 cm across, trumpet- or horn-shaped when young, later shaped like a deep cup, gradually tapering at the base; brown, yellowish-brown, the colour of a nutshell, the margin as if white-encrusted, as though with clipped eyelashes. Characteristic features: margin of the fruiting body as if encrusted, grows only on burnt ground. Grows in groups. Uncommon. Very similar is Tarzetta cupularis, but it is paler, cream-coloured, and grows on damp soil in forests, parks and shrublands.

ankstyvasis-nuosedis.features: Cap, gills and stem characteristically tinged violet
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 3-8 (10) cm across, convex-flattened, irregularly depressed, with a blunt umbo, fading, shiny, finely scaly, dark brown, purplish-brown, the margin often with a violet tinge, and the very edge with a rim of white veil. Gills purplish-brown, later with a violet tinge, old ones reddish-brown, broad, adnate. Stem 3–10 (15)x0.5-1.5 cm, of even thickness, club-shaped, violet, later whitish with only the base violet, faintly zigzag-banded yellowish-white. Flesh brownish, violet in the stem, not bitter. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies fragile, gills fairly broad, sparse. Grows singly or in small groups, especially in damp spruce forests. Inedible.

apgaulingasis-pumpotaukslis.features: Young fruiting bodies yellowish-orange, old ones brown
desc: Fruiting bodies small, 2-4 cm across, fibrous, shaggily warty, globose when young, later pear-shaped, the upper part (the head) wider, narrowing towards the base into a tapering stem. Young fruiting bodies yellowish-orange, coppery-pinkish, old ones brown. Flesh brown. Characteristic features: the upper part of the fruiting body is yellowish-orange, reddish-copper in colour, which makes this puffball easy to distinguish from others. Grows in summer and autumn in coniferous and deciduous forests, singly or in twos or threes (Valkininkai forests, Varėna district). Should be classed as deserving protection.

apgaulusis-krekenis.habitat: On rotting coniferous, more rarely deciduous wood
desc: Plasmodium white or pink, immature sporangia red, mature ones yellowish-brown, pear-shaped, 0.6-1 mm across, with stalks 1-2 mm long. Characteristic features: young sporangia red, when mature they lighten to yellowish-brown. Grows on rotten wood. Common. A slime mould of impressive appearance, like a string of mother-of-pearl beads.

apykaklinis-mazunis.features: Cap creamy white, pleated, stem reddish-brown, almost black
desc: Fruiting bodies tiny. Cap 0.5–1.5 cm across, flattened-convex, always with a narrow pit pressed in the centre, pleated-furrowed, white, creamy white. Gills distant, thick, white, yellowish when old, attached to a collar that is not attached to the stem, like a collar. Stem 2-6 cm long, up to 1.5 pm thick, thread-like, blackish, dark reddish-brown. Flesh membranous, very thin, whitish. Characteristic features: in dry weather the fruiting bodies seem to wither, reviving after rain. Grows in small groups. Fairly common. Inedible. A valuable litter saprotroph.

asarojanti-jaunabude.habitat: Coniferous and deciduous forests, roadsides, parks, shrublands, gardens
asarojanti-jaunabude.features: Gills yellowish-brown, spores large, a fungus with a persistent smell
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 3-8 cm across, whitish, pale yellowish-brownish, yellowish, dry, not slimy. Gills greyish-brownish, yellowish-brown, edges white-spotted, adnate. Stem 3–7 (9)x0.5–1.5 cm, white, near the gills as if mealy or powdered. Flesh whitish, with an unpleasant smell of old radishes, slightly bitter. Characteristic features: always grows in groups, the cap is the colour of coffee with milk. Inedible; the literature states that it is poisonous. Very common. Similar to the spring Calocybe, but that one is more massive, smells of flour, has whitish, yellowish gills and grows only in spring.

asutinis-mazunis.habitat: On fallen pine and spruce needles, more rarely on small twigs
asutinis-mazunis.features: Similar is Gymnopus perforans, but that one is larger and has a rough stem
desc: Fruiting bodies very small. Cap 0.3-0.7 (1) cm across, convex when young, later flattened, slightly depressed in the middle, matt, wrinkled, brownish, flesh-coloured, the margin paler, pleated. Gills narrow, distant, greyish, brownish, adnexed. Stem 3-8 cm long, of the shape and thickness of a horsehair, smooth, shiny, dark brown, almost black, paler near the gills. Flesh membranous, tough, without smell or taste. Characteristic features: tiny fungi growing only on fallen needles, more rarely on tiny twigs, as if sown over the forest litter. Grows in colonies. A valuable litter saprotroph. Inedible. Very widespread.

Fruiting bodies small – up to 4 cm across, almost globose when young, cup-shaped, finally irregular, wavy saucer-shaped. Upper surface slightly wrinkled, pale brown, yellowish-greyish-brown; underside brown, as if mealy, later the upper and lower sides become pale brown or the same colour, fading to grey. Flesh yellowish, fragile. There is no stem. Characteristic features: upper surface of the fruiting body somewhat wrinkled. Grows singly or in small groups on humus-rich soil, on decaying plant remains, in open places. Uncommon.

auksavirse-kartekle.habitat: Forests, parks, on rotten coniferous, more rarely deciduous wood
auksavirse-kartekle.features: Cap and gills mostly yellow, stem brownish
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 3-8 cm across, convex-flattened, surface smooth, rarely fibrous, dry, golden, reddish-yellow. Gills pale yellow, reddish-yellow when mature, rust-spotted, notched, edges white-toothed, notched, semi-decurrent. Stem 3-8x0.3-1 cm, slightly thickening towards the base, yellowish, reddish-brown when old, tough. Flesh yellowish, smelling of wood, bitter. Characteristic features: cap not scaly, grows mostly only on rotten coniferous wood. Appears as several fruiting bodies together. Inedible, common.

austriskoji-placiataure.habitat: Forest edges, forests, parks, bogs, groves, gardens
austriskoji-placiataure.features: A very beautiful, earliest spring fungus
desc: An early spring fungus and harbinger. Cap 1-5 (6) cm across, shaped like a wide goblet, inside a beautiful orange-red, outside whitish, yellowish, as if mealy. Stem 1-3x0.3-0.5 cm, widening upwards, merging into the cap, whitish. Flesh thin, pinkish, without any particular smell or taste. Grows as soon as the snow has melted, singly or in groups, on branches and twigs of deciduous trees, sometimes even with one end submerged in water, in groves, small pine woods and thickets. Very common. Inedible, but with a wonderfully beautiful cap. Estonians mention that in some countries this fungus is eaten.

Fungi perennial, large, 5–30 cm across, up to 10 cm thick. Fruiting bodies hoof-shaped, firmly attached to the tree by the side. Surface of young fruiting bodies smooth, later rough, knobbly, zoned, greyish, yellowish, chestnut-coloured, blackish-brown. Pores round, very small, yellowish-brown, ochre. Flesh hard, woody, yellowish-brown. Grows on trunks of living oaks, rarely on snags and stumps, very rarely on other deciduous trees. A harmful parasite, causing a yellowish white rot of the wood. More common in old-growth forests and parks.

azuoline-kreivabude.habitat: Parks, roadsides, on damaged parts of living deciduous trees
azuoline-kreivabude.features: Cap fleshy, firm, surface rough, fibrous-scaly
desc: Fruiting bodies large. Cap 3-13 (20) cm across, semicircular and broadly fan-shaped when young, later flattened, slightly depressed, fibrous, scaly, the margin bent downwards, with remnants of the membranous veil, white, grey, yellowish. Gills white, cream, yellowish, decurrent, edges not toothed. Stem 2-6x1-4 cm, eccentric, lateral, hairy, white, yellowish. Flesh firm, white, with a pleasant, piquant smell and a nutty taste. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies broadly fan-shaped, whitish-grey, flesh fleshy, with a piquant smell. Grows singly on deciduous, rarely on coniferous trees (at a damaged spot) or on dead wood. Inedible, not rare.

azuolinis-skiautenelis.habitat: On dead deciduous wood, especially oak stumps and snags
azuolinis-skiautenelis.features: Saprotroph of deciduous wood, spores amyloid
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 1-3 (4) cm across, kidney-, fan- or shell-shaped, eccentric, fibrous, scaly, depressed at the lateral stem, ochre-yellowish-brown, brownish-yellowish, fading to greyish. Gills thin, crowded, brownish-yellow, brownish, adnate. Stem 1-2x0.3-0.3 cm, tapering at the base, fibrous, eccentric, the colour of the gills. Flesh leathery, tough, ochre-yellowish, with a pleasant smell and a sharp, slightly bitter taste. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies leather-yellow, stem eccentric, grows mostly only on dead oak wood. Appears in small groups. Very common. Wood saprotroph. Inedible or even poisonous.

azuolinis-vinguris.habitat: On rotten oak and some other deciduous wood
azuolinis-vinguris.features: Most often grows only on oak
desc: Fruiting bodies large, perennial. Cap 5-10 (20) cm across, 2-5 cm thick. Fruiting bodies corky, in the form of lateral caps (brackets), surface uneven, zoned, rough, pale brown, yellowish, greyish-brown, sometimes turning greenish when overgrown with algae. Tubes labyrinthine, formed by gills fused together by anastomoses. Flesh pale brown, corky. Characteristic features: hymenophore labyrinthine.
Grows on dead, rarely living deciduous trees, especially on oak stumps. Occurs on chestnuts, beeches, walnut. Very common, causes an active brown rot. An active saprotroph.

baltaplause-sakabude.features: Small, fragile, fibrous fruiting bodies, cap not furrowed
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 1–3 cm across, convex, flattened when mature, pale cinnamon-coloured, the central part darker, fading, with white flakes. Gills at first pale brownish, later orange-brown, adnate. Stem 2-4x0.1-0.4 cm, fragile, the colour of the cap. Flesh brownish, thin.

Characteristic features: yellowish-brown fruiting bodies, growing on rotten wood debris. Appears in small groups in brighter places, on wood fragments, splinters and chips. Common. Wood saprotroph. Inedible.

baltasis-baltikas.features: White, greyish fruiting bodies, grows in groups, especially under birches
desc: Fruiting bodies large. Cap 8-12 cm across, irregularly flattened, matt, fibrous, white, turning brownish or yellowish with age, firm. Gills white, crowded, firm, brittle, adnate. Stem 7-12x0.5-1.5 cm, firm, fibrous, white, turning brownish with age. Flesh firm, white, with a pungent smell of rotten wood or gas, bitter. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies with an unpleasant smell and bitter taste. Grows in groups, often in rings around a birch, in deciduous and mixed forests, thickets, among grass. Common. Inedible. Similar to it is the true white knight (T. columbetta), but that one is fleshier, white and spotted pinkish. Rare. Edible. In Lithuania 31 species of Tricholoma have been found, of which 5 are mildly poisonous and 16 edible.

baltavirsunis-elniagrybis.habitat: Forests, parks, gardens, on rotten deciduous wood
baltavirsunis-elniagrybis.features: Perithecia-bearing bodies black, branched, branched tips white
desc: Perithecial stromata small, 3–5 (8) cm tall and 5 pm thick, cylindrical when young, later irregularly contorted, blackish-brown, black when old, widened in the upper part, branched like deer antlers, with pointed tips whitened by conidia. Stem woody, hard, black, rough. Flesh tough, hard, without any particular smell or taste. Characteristic features: spores black, half the size of those of Dead Man's Fingers. Grows in small groups and tufts. Very common, much more common than Dead Man's Fingers. An active saprotroph.

berzinis-pintenis.features: A white, soft, corky bracket, grows only on dead birches
desc: Fruiting bodies annual, large, solitary, round, hoof-shaped, cushion-like, slightly convex knob-like, attached to the substrate laterally or by a very short stem, white, greyish, greyish-yellowish, soft. Tubes white, cream, straw-coloured. Pores white, soon becoming yellowish, yellowish-brown when old. Flesh white, soft, spongy, corky. Grows in forests, parks, bogs and tussock swamps on birch snags, windfalls, dead branches and stumps, singly or a dozen or so fruiting bodies close to one another. A saprotroph, causing an active brown rot of the wood. Very common, an active decomposer of dead birch wood. A good forest sanitiser. It has attracted the interest of physicians.

bukagalvis-pirstunis.features: A fungus resembling a large, blunt-headed, yellowish-brown club
desc: Fruiting bodies large, shaped like a blunt club. Club 6-12 (15) cm tall, the upper part 3-7 cm across at its widest, the lower part gradually tapering to the base; surface smooth or slightly furrowed, velvety yellowish, orange, pale brown or with a pink tinge. Flesh firm, corky, whitish, darkening when broken or cut, taking on a brownish-violet tinge, mild-tasting. Characteristic features: similar to the giant club (Clavariadelphus pistillaris), but the head looks as if cut off, blunt, and the stem is shorter. Grows only in coniferous forests. Inedible. The largest club fungus, found only once in a mixed spruce forest, Gudeliai area, Marijampolė district. Deserves protection.

dantytalakste-gijabude.habitat: Meadows, pastures, open places, among grass
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 2-3 (4) cm across, conically convex-flattened, narrowly depressed in the centre, surface rough, finely scaly, bluish-black, violet-blue, violet-brown. Gills whitish, pale dark blue, with a greyish-pink tinge when old, edges blackish-blue toothed, adnexed. Stem 3–7x0.1–0.4 cm, dark blue, whitish-hairy at the base. Flesh greyish-blue. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies blackish-blue, cap depressed in the middle. Grows in small groups among grass in meadows, pastures and open places. Inedible. Rare.

demetoji-plempe.habitat: Coniferous forests, especially old mossy pine forests
demetoji-plempe.features: Cap white, yellowish, rust-spotted, very bitter taste
desc: Fruiting bodies medium to large. Cap 5-10 cm across, flattened, with a blunt umbo, matt, firm, white, whitish, yellowish-white with reddish-brown spots. Gills very crowded, narrow, white, yellowish, rust-spotted, adnate or free. Stem 5-10 (12)x1-2 cm, cartilaginous, twisted, firm, white, tapering at the base. Flesh fairly thick, firm, white, with an unpleasant smell and bitter taste. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies white, yellowish, firm, tough, spores round, small. Grows singly or in small groups. Inedible because of its bitterness. Common. Similar to white-coloured knights (Tricholoma), but, being of firm consistency, it is easily recognised. Inedible.

dirvonine-laibabude.habitat: Sandy, grassy soils, roadsides, riverbanks, forest clearings
dirvonine-laibabude.features: Fruiting bodies the colour of wet sand, cap depressed, gills distant
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 1-2 (3) cm across, depressed, with a smooth surface, the margin furrowed, pale reddish-brown, pinkish, the colour of human skin. Gills distant, the colour of the cap, clearly decurrent. Stem central, 1-3.3x0.1-0.3 cm, sometimes thickened at the base, the colour of the cap or somewhat paler. Flesh thin, brownish, without any particular smell or taste. Characteristic features: grows in sandy places: fallow land, squares, parks. Grows singly or in groups, mostly in autumn. Very common. Inedible.

dulkancioji-kremble.habitat: Dead fruiting bodies of brittlegills and milkcaps
dulkancioji-kremble.features: Fungi growing on other dead fungi, most often on brittlegills
desc: Fruiting bodies tiny. Cap 1–2 cm across, hemispherical when young, later flattened-convex, white, as if mealy, eventually turning brown (from chlamydospores), cracking, the margin bent downwards. Gills distant, thick, narrow, disappearing, or only rudiments of them are present. Stem 0.5-3x0.3-0.5 cm, usually bent, white, downy. Flesh thin, whitish, fragile, with an unpleasant smell of flour. Characteristic features: grows only on dead fruiting bodies, most often of brittlegills and milkcaps. Warmth-loving.

dvispalve-skujagalve.features: Cap slimy, redder in the middle, yellow at the margin
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 3-7 (10) cm across, flattened, with a blunt umbo, sometimes slightly depressed, sticky in wet weather, the central part orange-brown, rusty-red, pinkish, the margin more yellow. Gills yellowish, cream, later brownish-greyish-brown, crowded, broad, adnate or semi-decurrent. Stem 3-7x0.4-1 cm, of even thickness, greenish-yellowish at the top, reddish-brown lower down, fibrous. Flesh yellowish, mild-tasting. Characteristic features: grows in coniferous forests on rotten spruce and pine wood. Appears in small groups. Uncommon. Inedible.

dvokiancioji-gijabude.features: Fruiting bodies with an unpleasant smell of ammonia, spores angular
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 5-9 cm across, irregularly wavy-flattened or slightly depressed, grey, greyish-brownish, with a yellowish-greenish tinge. Young gills whitish, soon becoming pink, reddish-brown, distant, adnate. Stem 5-9x0.5-1 cm, fragile, greyish, greyish-brownish. Flesh greyish, thin, fragile, not bitter, with a strong smell of ammonia and stale flour. Characteristic features: greyish-brownish fruiting bodies, similar to the odourless pinkgill (Entoloma inodorum), but stinking. Grows in the same places as the odourless pinkgill. Inedible. Common.

dvokiancioji-smirdekle.habitat: On fallen, rotten branches of hazel, oak and other deciduous trees
dvokiancioji-smirdekle.features: Very tough, strongly stinking, small fungi
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 1-3 (4) cm across, convex, later flattened, depressed in the middle, irregularly pleated-wavy, wrinkled, furrowed, slimy, reddish-brown, brown, yellowish-brown. Gills distant, narrow, with anastomoses at the base, semi-decurrent. Stem 1-3 (5)x0.2-0.5 cm, very tough, velvety, blackish-brown, firmly attached to the substrate. Flesh thin, membranous, with a pungent smell of garlic and rotten fish, not bitter. Characteristic features: cap reddish-brown, stem blackish-brown, velvety. Grows mostly in groups, sometimes singly, close to one another, on fallen branches of deciduous trees. Not rare; in some oak woods very widespread.

dvokiancioji-zvynabudele.habitat: Thickets, roadsides, parks, forests, grassy places
dvokiancioji-zvynabudele.features: Cap umbrella-shaped, with reddish-brown scales on a white background
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 2-5 (7) cm across, thin-fleshed, fragile, white, shaggy with small brown, reddish-brown scales. Gills white, with brownish-spotted edges. Stem 3-7x0.3-0.5 cm, white, with a ring, yellowish-brownish below the ring. Flesh white, with a pleasant smell, not bitter. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies with an unpleasant, pungent smell. Spores blunt at the basal end, with a small beak. Grows in groups. Inedible. Very common.

dvokiantysis-plempis.features: Stem white-hairy, bristly, flesh with an unpleasant smell
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 3-5 (6) cm across, flattened, sometimes with an umbo, not fleshy, yellowish-brownish, the margin furrowed. Gills cream. Stem 3-6x0.5-0.7 cm, smooth near the gills, whitish, yellowish, brownish, white-hairy (bristly), evenly thickening towards the base. Flesh tough, juicy, white, smelling of garlic and rotten cabbage, not bitter.

Fruiting bodies tiny. Cap 0.5–1.5 (2) cm across, hemispherical when young, later flattened, slightly raised, spiny-scaly, reddish-brown, brick- or cinnamon-coloured. Gills reddish-brown, adnate. Stem 0.5–2x0.2–0.3 cm, fibrous, finely scaly, the colour of the cap. Flesh pale brown. Characteristic features: cap and stem fibrous-scaly, reddish-brown. Grows mostly in autumn on dead small twigs of willow, aspen and other deciduous trees, singly or in small groups. Uncommon. Inedible, a small but attractive-looking fungus.

egline-lempele.habitat: On dead coniferous, more rarely deciduous wood
egline-lempele.features: Fruiting bodies grey, yellowish, margins violet
desc: Fruiting bodies annual, small, 1-4 cm across, densely arranged in overlapping tiers, attached to the substrate by the edge, sometimes almost fully attached with only the margins raised from the substrate, or completely attached (resupinate), spreading; surface concentrically furrowed, covered with soft hairs, whitish, grey, yellowish, margins violet. Hymenophore whitish, later violet, violet-purple, cocoa-coloured, even brown. Tubes short (up to 2 mm), with toothed edges, fragile. Flesh very thin, leathery. Grows in forests and parks on fallen spruce and pine trunks, sometimes on stumps and snags, also occurring on aspens, hazels, birches and alders. Causes a fibrous white rot of the wood. Very common. An active saprotroph.

gauruotoji-plutpinte.habitat: On dead wood of deciduous, rarely coniferous trees
gauruotoji-plutpinte.season: From early spring to late autumn, even in winter
gauruotoji-plutpinte.features: Fruiting bodies leathery, coarsely hairy, felt-like
desc: Fruiting bodies spreading, usually forming semicircular caps 0.5-2 cm across, attached to the substrate by the side. Caps leathery, covered with dense, coarse hairs, grey, brownish in the middle, yellow towards the edges, with barely visible concentric zones. Hymenophore smooth, pale yellow, ochre, greyish-yellowish. Characteristic features: underside of the cap yellow, smooth. Grows on standing and fallen dead deciduous trees, branches, snags, more rarely stumps, also occurring on conifers. Causes a white rot of the wood. Very common. A good forest sanitiser. In rare cases a biotroph.

Fruiting bodies large, fleshy. Cap 8-15 (20) cm across, massive, whitish, cream, scaly, fibrous, and the margin strongly white-shaggy. Gills greyish-brown, later chocolate-coloured, adnate. Stem 5-7 (9)x1.5–5 cm, white, white-fibrous, shaggy. Characteristic features: massive fruiting bodies, stem short, thick, shaggy, flesh up to 3 cm thick, with an unpleasant smell and bitter taste. Grows in small groups, favouring abraded, damaged places of roadside trees, as well as of aspens (poplars), snags and stumps. Although very fleshy, it is inedible. Uncommon. A wood saprotroph, an impressive, attractive fungus, just don't hurry to put it in your basket.

gelsvarudis-mazunis.features: Stem with a sheath of yellow mycelium at the base
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 2–3 cm across, hemispherical when young, later flattened, with an umbo, somewhat wrinkled, yellowish-brown, surface finely velvety. Gills cream, adnexed. Stem 6-8x0.2–0.6 cm, whitish near the gills, reddish-brown lower down, yellow-hairy at the base, with a conspicuous felt-like yellow coating. Flesh whitish, without any particular smell or taste. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies tough, cystidia brown, large. Grows in small groups on rotten leaves, rarely needles. Inedible. Uncommon.

gelsvasis-zagarenis.habitat: Coniferous and deciduous forests, forest edges
desc: Fruiting bodies 3-7 cm tall, straight, unbranched, almost cylindrical, with blunt tips, yellow or orange-yellow. Stem short, slightly paler than the upper part of the fruiting body. Flesh yellowish, without any particular smell, slightly bitter-tasting. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies cylindrical, with blunt tips. Grows singly or in small groups, in forests among grass, in pastures, on fallow land, favouring grassy, brighter places. Inedible. Rare, only 3 sites are known (two in Marijampolė district and one in Klaipėda district). It should be looked for in other forests too and should be classed as protected.

gelsvoji-laibabude.habitat: In boggy places on peat hummocks with dead mosses
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 1-3 cm across, depressed, goblet-shaped, pale yellow, greenish-cream, the margin lobed-furrowed, pleated. Gills distant, whitish, whitish-yellowish, decurrent. Stem up to 2 cm long, central, the colour of the cap, paler at the base. Flesh very thin, yellowish, without any particular smell or taste. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies greyish, brownish-yellow, growing only in boggy places. Appears singly in swampy forests and bogs, on peaty soil, sometimes on rotted wood. Common. Inedible.

geltonasis-fuligas.habitat: On rotting wood, leaves, grass stems, needles
desc: Aethalia (fruiting bodies) yellow, from 1 to 15 cm across, sometimes larger, of irregular shape. The slimy mass is whitish, yellowish, covered with a calcareous, fragile peridium (skin). The capillitium consists of a network of colourless threads filled with calcareous amorphous granules. Characteristic features: a migrating plasmodium that changes colour, shape and consistency. Beautiful but unpleasantly slimy, sticky, yellow, sulphur-yellow plasmodia (like lumps of flakes) form on rotten wood and herbaceous plants. Common in forests, parks, forest edges and thickets. Inedible.

Fruiting bodies small. Cap 2-5 (7) cm across, convex, later convex-flattened, the centre slightly depressed, very fragile, thin-fleshed, pale yellow, ochre-yellow. Gills white, later yellowish, cream, brown-spotted, adnate. Stem 3-6x0.5-1.5 cm, white, yellowish-brownish when old. Flesh thin, fragile, slightly bitter-tasting, smelling of mustard. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies smell of mustard, grow only under beeches, oaks, birches and limes. Grows in summer and autumn, singly or in small groups. Not used as food because of its bitter taste. Rare.

geltonoji-baltekle.habitat: Deciduous, coniferous and mixed forests, damp grassy places
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 2–4 (6) cm across, flattened, matt, fibrous, smooth-surfaced when old, golden-yellow, brownish-yellow. Gills narrow, crowded, yellow, adnate. Stem 3-7x0.3-0.8 cm, fibrous, yellow, whitish at the base. Flesh thin, soft, yellow, smelling of flour, not bitter. Characteristic features: small, yellow fungi smelling of flour, spores tiny, non-amyloid. Grows singly or a few fruiting bodies together, in forests and parks among grass, on the ground. Rare, inedible. Deceptive – it sometimes makes you bend down as if it were a chanterelle.

geltonraude-kelmabude.features: Cap clearly white-fibrous, especially at the margin
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 3–10 (12) cm across, surface smooth, yellowish-red, the margin paler, with a conspicuous yellowish-greyish concentric rim of fibrils. Young gills greyish-cream, old ones dark greenish-brown, adnate. Stem yellowish-brown, without a ring, woody, 3-10 cm long and up to 1.3 cm thick. Flesh yellowish, firm, bitter-tasting, smelling of wood. Characteristic features: cap brick-red, margin paler, with a fairly conspicuous concentric rim of greyish-yellow fibrils. Grows in groups on dead deciduous wood – windfalls, snags, stumps. Fairly common. According to some authors it is edible, according to others inedible. Not recommended.

geltonrude-kartekle.habitat: On rotten coniferous and deciduous wood
geltonrude-kartekle.features: Cap, gills and stem predominantly yellow
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 3-6 cm across, convex, flattened when mature, sometimes with an umbo, ochre-yellow, reddish-yellow, fading to brownish. Young gills bright yellow, later yellowish-brown, notched. Stem 3–6x0.3–1 cm, of even thickness, yellowish-brown, with an inconspicuous ring-like remnant. Flesh yellowish, firm, thin, with a pleasant smell and bitter taste. Characteristic features: cap yellow-fibrous, stem with a ring-like remnant. Grows singly or a few fruiting bodies together. Inedible, uncommon.

graziakotis-baravykas.habitat: Deciduous and coniferous forests, favours the vicinity of oaks and hornbeams
graziakotis-baravykas.features: Stem of even thickness, red at the bottom, flesh bitter, turning bluish
desc: Fruiting bodies rather stout, fleshy. Cap 10–15 cm across, grey, dirty brownish-grey, matt. Pores bright yellow, turning slightly blue when pressed. Stem up to 3 cm thick, yellow in the upper part, beautifully red lower down, with a net. Flesh yellowish, turning bluish when cut, with an unpleasant bitter taste. Characteristic features: stem with a yellow net in the upper part and a red net in the lower part. Grows singly. Inedible because of its bitter taste, but not poisonous. Found very rarely, protected. Beautiful, attractive.

Fruiting bodies small. Cap 3-7 cm across, convex, raised-flattened, flattened, with an umbo, lemon-, sulphur-yellow, flame-coloured, sticky, scaly, fibrous. Gills the colour of the cap, greenish-yellow, yellowish-brown, adnate. Stem 3–8x0.3-0.8 cm, with a ring-like zone, the colour of the cap and likewise shaggy. Flesh yellow, fairly thick, slightly bitter-tasting. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies as if bristling, scaly, sulphur-yellow. Grows on rotten coniferous wood, windfalls and snags, singly or a few fruiting bodies together, which is uncharacteristic of stumpcaps. Inedible. Common.

gurusis-rusiagrybis.habitat: On rotten coniferous and deciduous wood
gurusis-rusiagrybis.features: Fruiting bodies with white downy margins, spores large
desc: Fruiting bodies spreading (resupinate). When young they are small, irregularly round, later several grow together and spread into a large, pale brown, brown, brownish-violet, fleshy film that separates easily from the substrate, its surface with brown granules and small warts, and the margins loose, downy, white. Grows in (abandoned) wooden buildings, timber stores without ventilation, and in forests on windfalls and stumps. One of the most dangerous house fungi, destroying wood and causing much damage. Very common.

Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 5-10 cm across, conical, later flattened with a blunt umbo, very slimy, shiny, pale ochre, straw-coloured, yellowish-reddish-brown, with a greenish tinge, the margin paler, with remnants of a white slimy veil. Gills greyish-violet, old ones reddish-brown. Stem 5–10x1-2 cm, white, later yellowish-brownish, sheathed in a slimy white veil which turns brown from fallen spores and cracks, mottling the stem with snake-skin zigzags. Flesh cream, white, thin, without any particular smell or taste. Characteristic features: stem roughly mottled with zigzags. Grows singly or in small groups, favouring the vicinity of birch, oak and aspen. Inedible, uncommon.

issetinis-meslagrybis.features: Tiny fungi growing only on rotten wood
desc: Delicate, tiny fruiting bodies. Cap 0.5-1 (2) cm across, furrowed, somewhat pleated, white-fibrous, brownish-grey, yellowish. Gills greyish, old ones brownish-black. Stem 2–3x0.1–0.15 cm, white, very fragile. Flesh thin, without any particular smell. Characteristic features: grows in large colonies, groups and tufts on and around rotten snags, windfalls and stumps. Grows in summer and autumn. Saprotroph, inedible. Very common. A good sanitiser of nature, a brisk decomposer of rotting wood.

ivairiaspalve-kempe.habitat: Old stumps, windfalls and snags of deciduous trees
desc: Annual fruiting bodies, up to 12 cm across, a rosette of round, fan-shaped caps, usually fused together in overlapping tiers. Cap surface velvety, hairy, with concentric yellowish, brownish, brown, reddish-brown, bluish and greyish-black zones. Tubes white, up to 2 pm long. Flesh white, thin, leathery.
Grows in forests and parks, sometimes in gardens, on dead deciduous wood.
Causes a white rot of the wood. Very common. Sometimes the rosettes of caps touch or even fuse, covering the whole stump and decorating it as if with beautiful large buttons that inspire admiration.

izulnusis-skylenis.habitat: On living birches, rarely on other deciduous trees, at damaged spots
izulnusis-skylenis.features: Sterile growths large, bluish-black, developing from spores
desc: Growths 10-30 cm across and larger, irregularly cracked, fissured outgrowths, brown, bluish-black in colour. This sterile, spore-less form of Inonotus obliquus is the only one usually seen in our forests – growths on birches. The fruiting bodies are under the tree bark, invisible. Annual, widely spreading, soft and leathery when young, later fibrous, dried, hard and brittle, consisting almost entirely of tubes. Tubes single-layered, oblique, 3-5 mm long, whitish when young, tobacco-coloured when old. Pores angular. In Lithuania only a few sites are known. Characteristic features: the fruiting bodies are usually seen only after the birch has fallen. Grows in forests, bogs and parks. Has medicinal properties.

juodkote-meskute.habitat: Rotten spruce and pine wood, decayed stumps, snags, windfalls
juodkote-meskute.features: Cap eccentric, stem short, black-velvety, eccentric
desc: Fruiting bodies large, massive. Cap grows up to 25 cm across and larger, velvety, reddish-brown, yellowish-brown, massive, fleshy. Gills yellowish, pinkish-yellowish, crowded, broad, soft. Stem short, thick (2-6x2-4 cm), velvety, lateral, almost black. Flesh yellowish, firm, soft when old, not bitter. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies massive, appearing on rotten coniferous wood. Grows in coniferous and mixed forests, usually singly, rarely several fruiting bodies together. Inedible. Uncommon.

karcioji-postija.habitat: Most often spruce, rarely deciduous stumps, windfalls, snags
desc: Fruiting bodies annual, small, up to 6-8 cm across, semicircular, fan-shaped or of other shape, usually attached to the substrate by a broad side, soft, watery, surface finely shaggy, uneven, wrinkled, warty, cream, pale ochre or faded. Hymenophore white, cream, yellowish. Tubes white, soft, in wet weather exuding droplets of colourless liquid. Pores small, round or angular. Flesh soft, juicy, white, bitter, with a burning taste and an unpleasant smell of rot. Grows in forests and parks on conifers, rarely on deciduous trees. Causes an active reddish (brown) rot of the wood. Very common. An active saprotroph.

karpiniuotoji-gleiviabude.habitat: Base of living aspens, rarely stumps, snags
desc: Fruiting bodies medium to large. Cap 3-10 cm across, growing even larger, surface with a thick layer of slime, yellowish-brown scaly, violet-brown, chestnut-coloured when old. Gills violet-brown, chocolate-coloured, the edges of young ones with white sticky droplets. Stem 3-13x0.3-4 cm, greyish, covered with brown fibrils and small scales, with a ring. Flesh yellowish, thick, firm, bitter-tasting. Characteristic features: grows only at the base of aspen, rarely on other trees; gill edges of young fungi with white sticky droplets, old ones white-spotted. Grows singly or 2-7 fruiting bodies together. Not rare in Lithuania, very rare in many countries. Inedible. A parasite, in places dangerous to aspen stands.

kartusis-baravykas.habitat: Parks, deciduous forests, especially calcareous oak woods with hornbeam and lime
kartusis-baravykas.features: Stem tapering like a root, flesh bitter, turning bluish
desc: Fruiting bodies large, fleshy. Cap grows up to 25 cm across, grey, yellowish-brownish, yellowish-grey. Tubes dirty yellowish, pores grey, yellow, turning blue when pressed. Stem swollen in the middle to 8 cm thick, tapering like a root at the base, with a brownish net. Flesh yellow, turning blue when broken, bitter-tasting.
Characteristic features: pores grey, yellow, stem bulging in the middle, tapering at the base, ending in a rhizoid.
Grows singly in deciduous forests, especially in calcareous, clayey oak woods. Inedible because of its bitter taste. Rarely found. Protected.

Fruiting bodies small. Cap 1.5–3 cm across, depressed, fibrous, scaly, rough, the surface of old ones smooth, greyish, dark greyish-brown, the margin furrowed. Gills pale greyish-brown, adnate, semi-decurrent. Stem 3-4x0.2-0.5 cm, thickening towards the base, the colour of the cap, white-downy at the base. Flesh thin, greyish, not bitter, odourless. Characteristic features: appears singly or several fruiting bodies together on rotten stumps and snags of coniferous and deciduous trees. Very rare. Inedible.

keturskiautis-zvaigzdinas.features: When the exoperidium splits, the endoperidium is raised on 4 pointed rays
desc: Young fruiting bodies globose, closed, 2-4 cm across, leathery yellow, greyish-brown. When the exoperidium splits, its 4 pointed rays, resting on the ground as if on hands, lift up the ovoid-elongated, 2x1 cm, bluish-grey, later brown, almost black endoperidium, a small body with a neat opening at the top. Gleba blackish-brown. Grows in coniferous and mixed forests among and on fallen needles and leaves. An old-growth forest fungus. Rare. Protected.

kietoji-kempine.habitat: On living and dead deciduous trees, rarely on conifers
kietoji-kempine.features: Most often grows on willows, more rarely on birches, oaks and fruit trees
desc: A perennial fungus. Fruiting bodies up to 25 cm across, shaped like a horse's hoof (sometimes knob-like or irregular), woody, hard, firmly attached to the tree by the edge. Surface smooth, with narrow concentric grooves, cracked, matt or glossy, blackish-brown or even black. Tubes multi-layered, 3–5 mm long, pores round, small, yellowish-brown, covered with a greyish bloom. Flesh hard, woody, up to 2 cm thick. Grows singly or in small groups in forests, parks and gardens on living and dead trees. Causes a white or yellowish rot of the wood. Very common.
Similar to it is the aspen bracket (P. tremulae), which grows only on living aspens. It causes a whitish or yellowish rot of the wood. Both these fungi cause much damage.

Fruiting bodies medium-sized, 5-6 cm tall, club- or tongue-shaped. In the upper part, 1-3 cm high, the widened cap is irregularly tongue-shaped, club-shaped, wrinkled, matt, black. Stem 2-4 cm tall, round, flat, straight or curved, firm, tapering at the base. Characteristic features: grows among sphagnum mosses. Appears as a few fruiting bodies together in damp, swampy places among sphagnum. Very rare, deserves protection

kislusis-elniagrybis.habitat: Forests, parks, on rotten deciduous wood
kislusis-elniagrybis.features: Perithecial stromata club-shaped, spindle-shaped, black, flesh white
desc: Perithecial stromata small, 4-6 (8) cm tall and up to 2 cm thick, club-, finger- or spindle-shaped, shaped like a bent boxing glove, light brown, brown when young, brownish-black, black, violet-black when mature, granular, wrinkled-warty. Stem short. Flesh white, tough, corky, thick. Characteristic features: spores black, large. Grows singly or in groups. Not rare, inedible. The shape of the fruiting body varies greatly – from finger-like and cylindrical to the shape of a boxing glove and others. An active saprotroph.

Fruiting bodies small. Cap 1-3 (4) cm across, convex, later flattened, yellowish-brown, the margin paler, bent downwards. Gills brownish, later brown, adnexed. Stem 2-3x0.3-0.6 cm, of even thickness, the lower part deep in the sand, whitish near the gills, brownish, brown and greyish-fibrous below. Flesh thin, whitish, without any particular smell or taste. Characteristic features: grows only on dunes and mostly only in spring. Appears singly or several fruiting bodies together. Inedible. Rare. In Lithuania 31 species of Hebeloma have been recorded so far; there are no edible or poisonous ones, almost all are mycorrhizal, useful in the life of the forest and park.

kopine-trapiabude.features: Grows in sandy places, most often only on coastal dunes
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 1-3 (4) cm across, raised-flattened, matt, dirty brown, yellowish-brown, fading to pale brown, brownish or even whitish. Gills brownish, later becoming brown, blackish-brown, edges whitish, adnate. Stem 3-7x0.2-0.3 cm, the colour of the cap, deeply embedded in sand. Flesh without any particular smell or taste. Characteristic features: yellowish-brown fungi, stem deeply sunk in sand. Grows singly or in small groups. Rare, saprotroph. In Lithuania 47 species of Psathyrella have been found so far; from a practical point of view they are important as wood and litter saprotrophs, only a few species are edible – and those of little value; there are no poisonous ones.

koretoji-skyletbude.habitat: On rotten deciduous, very rarely coniferous wood
koretoji-skyletbude.features: Woody fruiting bodies, yellowish-brown, cap bristly
desc: Fruiting bodies small, annual. Cap 2-5 (6) cm across, raised-flattened, slightly depressed in the middle, yellowish, yellowish-brown, ochre-yellowish, fibrous, finely scaly, matt, tough. Tubes 1-2 pm long, slightly decurrent down the stem. Stem 1-3 (4)x2–5 cm, greyish, yellowish, finely scaly in the upper part, only fibrous lower down. Flesh thin, hard, white, without any particular smell or taste. Characteristic features: stem yellowish, scaly in the upper part. Grows singly or several fruiting bodies together, causes a white rot of the wood. Inedible, uncommon.

krateriskasis-taurunis.features: Funnel- or horn-shaped, brownish-black fruiting bodies
desc: Fruiting bodies 2-6 cm tall and 1-4 cm across, at first closed, globose, later, when the top opens, becoming deep goblet-, funnel- or horn-shaped, the margin cracked, fleshy, later of leathery consistency, surface felty, blackish-brown, blackish. Stem up to 4 cm long and 1 cm thick, hollow, widening towards the top, the colour of the cap. Characteristic features: although named a 'noble cup', it is a fungus of gloomy, mystical appearance. Grows singly, in groups, even large ones, on decaying wood and rotten leaves, favouring calcareous, humus-rich places. Inedible. One of the earliest spring fungi. Rare.

kraujaspalve-umede.features: Cap blood-red, fading, stem with a red bloom
desc: Medium-sized. Cap 5-10 cm across, matt, the cuticle peels with difficulty, dark red, blood-red, the margin more yellowish, spotted. Gills white, cream when old, adnate. Stem 3-7x2-3 cm, white, with a pink bloom. Flesh white, up to 2 cm thick, firm, bitter, with a fruity smell. Characteristic features: a typical pine-forest species, cap yellowish-spotted, the cuticle does not peel, only tears off at the margin. Grows singly or in small groups. Edible when well boiled, but not recommended because of its bitter taste; it is classed as inedible. Common.

kupstine-salmabude.habitat: Stumps and windfalls of oak, rarely other deciduous trees
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 1-3 cm across, conically bell-shaped, flattened when old, with a sharp umbo, translucently wrinkled-furrowed, reddish-brown, greyish-brown, yellowish-brown. Gills distant, thick, white, adnate. Stem 3–10 (12)x0.2-0.4 cm, whitish, yellowish, bright yellowish-brown, orange-brown towards the base. Flesh brownish, with a rather pungent smell of flour, wood or even cucumber, not bitter. Characteristic features: stem orange-, yellowish-brown, most often found on oak stumps. Grows in large groups, bunches and tufts (sometimes up to a hundred or more). Very common. A wood saprotroph, very active. Inedible.

kvapnioji-anyzpinte.habitat: On rotten conifers, especially spruce stumps, snags, windfalls
kvapnioji-anyzpinte.features: Fruiting bodies corky, surface felt-like, velvety
desc: Fruiting bodies large, perennial, 3-15 cm across, semicircular or cushion-shaped, sometimes several fused together. Surface uneven, velvety, felt-like, rough, from yellowish-brown to almost black, the margins thick, blunt, rounded, yellow, orange-yellow, sometimes greyish-yellow. Tubes pale yellowish, pores round, elongated, angular, labyrinthine, pale brown. Flesh pale brown, smelling of anise, with an unpleasant taste, corky. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies smell of anise. Grows in forests and parks, mostly on dead coniferous, rarely deciduous wood. Causes a reddish (brown) rot of the wood. Common. Saprotroph.

Fruiting bodies small. Cap 1-3.5 cm across, bell- or saddle-shaped, made up of 2-3 convex yellowish-brown, pale brown, greyish-brown lobes. Stem 3-6 (8)x0.3-0.6 (0.8) cm, thickening towards the base, smooth or sometimes slightly furrowed, yellowish, brownish. Flesh thin, greyish, fragile. Characteristic features: hymenium pale yellowish-brown, greyish-brown. Grows singly or in groups, favouring bright, open places. Not rare.

lapinis-mazunis.habitat: On fallen tree leaves, especially their petioles and veins, and on grass stems
desc: Fruiting bodies tiny, delicate. Cap 0.5-1 cm across, flattened, leathery, wrinkled, whitish, cream. Gills very narrow, branched-vein-like, thick, adnate, whitish. Stem up to 3 cm long, thread-like, brownish, white near the gills. Flesh very thin, membranous, without any particular smell or taste. Characteristic features: white, cream, delicate fruiting bodies growing on fallen leaves, especially their veins and petioles. Fairly common. A valuable litter saprotroph. Very similar is the aspen parachute (M. tremulae), but it grows only on aspen leaves and is also not rare. Inedible.

lapinis-pirstunelis.habitat: Forests, parks, grows on rotten leaf veins and petioles
lapinis-pirstunelis.features: Fertile part of the club white, sterile part reddish-brown
desc: Fruiting bodies tiny, consisting of a fertile and a sterile part. Fruiting body 1-3 cm tall, the head (fertile part) 0.5-1.5 cm long, up to 0.1 mm thick, white. Stem (sterile part) 1-2 cm long, 1-0.3 mm thick, tough, reddish-brown. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies tiny, two-coloured, growing from a sclerotium. Grows singly but close to one another, on last year's leaves of aspen, alder and other deciduous trees. Grows from a tiny sclerotium. Common. Saprotroph, an active decomposer of leaves.

Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 7-8 cm across, dry, matt, fibrous, ivory with a violet tinge, ochre-brownish when old. Young gills greyish, violet, bluish, later fading to yellowish-brown, adnate. Stem 5-12x0.5-2 cm, thickening towards the base, firm, white, whitish-violet when young, zigzag-fibrous with a ring-like remnant of the white veil. Flesh bluish, brownish in old fungi, with an unpleasant smell, not bitter. Characteristic features: cap, stem and flesh greyish-bluish-violet. Grows singly or in small groups, favouring the vicinity of oak. Inedible, common.

liaukingasis-drebutis.habitat: Rotten deciduous wood, especially aspen branches
desc: Fruiting bodies small, 3-6 cm across, usually several fused into lumps up to 30 cm long. Wavy-wrinkled, rough with tiny warts, the upper side shiny, tar-black; depending on location and lighting the colour may range from black to greyish; the underside matt, greyish-black, of jelly-like consistency. Flesh gelatinous, elastic, watery, without any particular smell or taste. Grows mostly in deciduous forests on fallen, broken branches, especially in late autumn and even in winter (down to -10 °C); it also occurs on coniferous branches

lygusis-tigliagrybis.features: Very similar to the fluted bird's nest, but yellow
desc: Fruiting bodies tiny. Young ones elongated-globose, later elongated, cylindrical, shaped like small crucibles or cups, 0.5–1.5 cm tall and 0.5–0.8 (1) cm wide, the outer side hairy, felty, yellow, yellowish-brown, lion-coloured, the inner side shiny, pale brown, greyish, smooth, not fluted. Peridioles numerous, as if heaped in a basket, flat, lens-shaped, containing spores. Grows in small groups, several to a dozen or more fruiting bodies, on rotten wood, straw and herbaceous debris. Common. Saprotroph.

Fruiting bodies small, tough, of jelly-like consistency, cylinder- or club-shaped, very rarely slightly branched, somewhat pointed in the upper part, 0.5-1.5 cm tall, pale yellow, brownish-yellow. Flesh yellowish. Characteristic features: somewhat similar to the yellow stagshorn (Calocera viscosa), but its fruiting bodies are small, growing close to one another in large colonies on windfalls, branches and stumps. Grows in larger or smaller groups in forests, parks, gardens and homestead sites on rotten wood. Not rare.

melsvalakstis-nuosedis.features: Stem white, bluish in the upper part
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 3–6 (8) cm across, raised-flattened, occasionally slightly depressed, sticky, shiny, yellowish-ochre, yellowish-brown, lemon-coloured. Gills crowded, greyish-violet, bluish-violet when young, brownish-rust when old, adnate. Stem 5-10x0.5-1 cm, thickening towards the base, up to 2 cm thick, white, bluish near the gills, yellowish when old, with brownish oblique stripes of the veil. Flesh thin, whitish-yellowish, without any particular smell or taste. Characteristic features: cap yellow, gills violet (when young), stem thickening towards the base. Grows singly or several fruiting bodies together, among mosses. Inedible, fairly common. In Lithuania 123 species of Cortinarius have been identified so far, all of them mycosymbiotrophs; only a few are edible, the others are inedible or poisonous, and 2-3 are deadly poisonous.

melsvejancioji-portija.features: Fruiting bodies greenish-bluish, turning blue when pressed
desc: Fruiting bodies annual. Caps semicircular, 2-7 cm wide, 1-5 cm across and up to 1 cm thick, growing singly or in small groups – several together, one above another. Surface rough, hairy, wrinkled-shaggy, faintly zoned, white, grey, soon becoming dirty greenish-blackish-blue. Underside white, whitish or cream, pores tiny, soon darkening, turning bluish immediately when pressed. Flesh soft, white, turning bluish. Characteristic features: its dirty-blue fruiting bodies easily distinguish it from other Postia species and make it easy to recognise. Grows only on dead coniferous, rarely deciduous wood, causing a brown rot of the wood. Not rare.

minkstasis-klumpiaausis.features: Most widespread on aspen windfalls, snags, stumps, branches
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 3–5 (7–9) cm across, horse-hoof-shaped when young, roundly or broadly fan-shaped when mature, the margin bent downwards, dirty grey, greyish-brownish, yellowish-brownish, the cuticle tough, elastic. There is no stem, or only an inconspicuous rudimentary remnant; attached to the substrate by the side. Flesh thick, soft, elastic, not bitter, the smell not strong. Characteristic features: the largest fungus of this genus, growing in large colonies on rotten wood. Appears on dead branches, windfalls and stumps of deciduous trees, very rarely singly, usually in colonies. Inedible, very common. A wood saprotroph, a sanitiser.

oranzine-laibunele.habitat: Forests, especially coniferous, parks, among mosses and grass
desc: Fruiting bodies tiny, minute. Cap 0.5-1.5 cm across, convex-flattened, depressed, surface smooth, yellowish-orange, fading to yellowish, the margin furrowed. Gills brownish, yellow, decurrent. Stem 3-6 (8)x0.1-0.2 cm, the colour of the cap. Flesh pale. Characteristic features: orange, minute fruiting bodies. Grows singly or in groups, only in forests. Very common. Saprotroph. Very similar is Rickenella setipes (Fr.) Raith., but its cap is reddish-brown and bluish-black in the centre. It appears in the same places.

oziakvapis-nuosedis.features: Cap and stem with a violet tinge, gills yellowish-brown
desc: Fruiting bodies massive. Cap 5-9 (13) cm across, fleshy, silky-fibrous, finely scaly, violet, fading to pale yellowish-brownish, ochre-yellowish. Gills yellowish, later reddish-brown, adnexed. Flesh yellow, with a bitter taste and an unpleasant specific (goat) smell. Stem 7-12x1-3 cm, violet when young, later greyish, thickening downwards, conspicuously fibrous. Characteristic features: the veil of young fruiting bodies violet, later yellowish-brown; the fungus has a specific, persistent goat smell. Grows singly or several fruiting bodies together, in spruce and pine forests, favouring mossy places. Inedible, not rare.

pakopine-antrodija.features: Fruiting body spreading, caps growing in overlapping tiers one above another
desc: Fruiting bodies annual, sometimes perennial, elongated-spreading. Thin caps growing in overlapping tiers one above another, up to 3 cm wide, 2 cm across, the surface lumpy, finely hairy, bristly, smooth, yellowish, brownish, ochre, and the margins blunt, zoned, white. Young hymenophore white, later yellowish, up to 0.7 cm thick, pores distinct, angular. Flesh white, corky, with a strong smell of sponge, not bitter. Characteristic features: the fruiting body consists of many tiny caps. Grows on spruce, occurring on pines, very rarely on deciduous stumps and windfalls; causes a brown rot of the wood, active, a xylotroph.

paprastasis-ausiadyglis.habitat: On fallen pine and spruce cones, in forests and parks
paprastasis-ausiadyglis.features: Grows only on pine, rarely on spruce cones; spores small
desc: Fruiting bodies tiny, small. Cap 0.5-1 (2.5) cm across, kidney-shaped, lateral, eccentric, semicircular, fan-shaped, dark brown, blackish-brown, shaggy with stiff brown bristles. Spines conical, up to 3 pm long, firm, brown, decurrent down the stem. Stem 1-5x0.1-0.2 cm, lateral, covered with brown hairs. Flesh tough, whitish, turning brown. Characteristic features: cap fan-shaped, brown and black bristly, stem hairy. Grows singly. Inedible. Very common. Saprotroph.

Perithecia (semi-closed type of fruiting bodies) tiny, round, 0.5-2 cm across, soft, of waxy consistency, hard when old, ruby-red, brownish-red, fading to brownish, pinkish, greyish-brownish; under a magnifying glass the surface looks as if wrinkled. Characteristic features: spores with one transverse central septum. Grows on almost all dead deciduous trees and shrubs, trunks and branches, in autumn, on warmer winter days and in spring. Fairly harmful to gardens – currants, raspberries, gooseberries, as well as fruit trees. Lives mostly as a saprotroph, more rarely as a biotroph. Very common.

paprastasis-taukius.features: Inside of the fruiting bodies of jelly-like consistency
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized, 3-8 (10) cm tall and 3-5 cm across, rarely larger, usually globose, shaped like a small barrel or a crock for keeping soured milk, but the inside is filled with a colourless jelly-like slime or slime resembling thick oil, so it is soft, as if made of rubber, with a dark brown, shiny saucer-shaped depression at the top; the outer surface is wrinkled like elephant skin, dark brown, fibrous, rough. Old fruiting bodies are shrivelled, shapeless. Characteristic features: they look like little rubber barrels among the needles. Grows in November and December or early in spring, as soon as the snow has melted, in old spruce forests, in groups, among mosses. Not found in recent years. Protected.

paprastasis-zaliagrybis.features: Bluish-green fruiting bodies, growing only on rotten wood
desc: Fruiting bodies tiny. Cap 0.3-0.8 cm across, round and closed when young, later shaped like a small goblet, saucer or bowl, irregularly wavy-flattened, depressed, surface smooth, green. Stem very short, up to 3 cm long and 0.3 mm thick, green. Flesh bluish, tough, thin. Grows on rotten deciduous and coniferous wood – stumps, snags, windfalls, fallen logs – in groups and colonies. The fungus stains the wood green, which is suitable for use in artistic woodcarving. Inedible.

paprastoji-alksniabude.habitat: On dead deciduous and coniferous wood
paprastoji-alksniabude.features: Woody fungi growing even in winter on days without frost
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 1-3 (3) cm across, fan- or shell-shaped, greyish, whitish-grey, soft cream, greyish-yellowish, surface bristly, similar to felt, the margin lobed and pleated. False gills radiating from the point of attachment to the substrate towards the cap margin, pinkish-brownish, violet-grey, ochre-brownish, the edges split lengthwise, as if doubled, distant. Flesh pale, thin, tough, without any particular smell, mild-tasting.

Characteristic features: fan-shaped, shaggy, felt-like fruiting bodies. Grows mostly on snags, dead branches and stumps, rarely on debarked, dried wood of living trees. It does not freeze to death or dry out; after rain it revives and continues to grow.

parazitinis-aksombaravykis.habitat: Living fruiting bodies of the common earthball (Scleroderma citrinum)
parazitinis-aksombaravykis.features: A parasite growing on the common earthball
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 3–7 cm across, velvety, matt, pale greenish-yellow, yellowish-brown, yellow-brown. Tubes yellow, later greenish-yellow, difficult to separate from the cap, pores the colour of the tubes. Stem 3-7x0.5-1 cm, yellowish, reddish-yellow, tapering towards the base. Flesh greyish, yellowish-grey, not bitter, with a faint mushroom smell. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies small, flesh does not change colour. Grows in forests, parks and gardens as a parasite. Very rare, inedible, although some sources state that it is edible. Warmth-loving. Protected.

pieniskoji-postija.habitat: On rotten deciduous and coniferous wood
pieniskoji-postija.season: From early spring to late autumn
pieniskoji-postija.features: Fruiting bodies white, cream, not turning brown, spores tiny
desc: Fruiting bodies annual, small, in the form of semicircular caps, usually attached to the substrate by the edge or a short stem, solitary, up to 6 cm across or several fused together, soft, watery, fleshy. Cap surface almost smooth, sometimes as if mealy, white, later becoming cream or yellowish. Flesh watery, white, tasteless, rarely slightly sour. Grows in forests, parks, sometimes gardens, on deciduous, rarely coniferous stumps, snags and windfalls. Causes a white rot of the wood. Very common. Saprotroph.

pievinis-meslagrybis.habitat: Meadows, forest edges, fallow land, pastures
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 0.5-1.5 cm across, conical when young, finally shaped like an open umbrella, very thin, translucent, pleated-grooved, grey, yellowish-brown in the centre, without signs of autolysis (does not drip away). Gills whitish, black when old, distant, narrow. Stem 3–5x0.1–0.2 cm, fragile, white. Flesh membranous, without smell or taste. Characteristic features: delicate fruiting bodies, cap shaped like an open umbrella, dries out in the meadow. Grows singly, more rarely several fruiting bodies together or in small groups, among grass. Common.

piktoji-skujagalve.habitat: Forests, parks, gardens, homesteads – on rotten wood
piktoji-skujagalve.features: Similar to the golden and sticky scalycaps, but smaller and less brown
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 3-5 cm across, convex, convex-flattened, slightly depressed, with or without a blunt umbo, sticky, orange-yellow, with reddish-brown scales. Gills pale brownish-yellow, adnate. Stem 2–6x0.3–0.8 cm, yellowish-white, fibrous, scaly. Flesh yellowish-brown, without any particular smell, slightly bitter-tasting. Characteristic features: orange-yellow, scaly cap, stem white, yellowish, scaly. Grows on rotten deciduous and coniferous wood, singly or in small groups. Rare. Inedible. Found even at homesteads, on wood debris and on log ends piled up for firewood.

piktoji-umede.features: Cap shiny when wet, matt when dry, red, blood-coloured
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 5-8 (10) cm across, flattened, slightly depressed in the middle, the cuticle peels easily, the margin furrowed. Gills white, cream when old, fragile, not broad, adnexed. Stem 5-8x1-2 cm, white. Flesh white, fragile, thin, with a sharp peppery taste. Characteristic features: gills white, cream when old, stem white, flesh very bitter. The cap colour varies with the habitat. Grows singly or in small groups, especially in damp places. Very common, inedible because of its bitter taste. In all, 300 species of Russula have been described, 200 in Europe, and in Lithuania so far 60. Almost all are edible; only the very bitter-tasting ones should not be eaten.

pilksvagelsve-umede.features: Cap fleshy, greyish-yellow, gills and stem yellowish
desc: Fruiting bodies medium to large. Cap convex-flattened, later flattened, even slightly depressed, sometimes with an umbo, matt, the cuticle adnate, peeling with difficulty, straw-coloured, yellowish-ochre, with a greyish tinge, the margin faintly pleated, furrowed. Gills pale, later becoming pale yellow, adnate. Stem 3-8x1-2 (3) cm, white, soon becoming yellowish, straw-coloured. Flesh thick (up to 1.3 cm), whitish, yellowish, smelling of rot and herring, bitter-tasting. Characteristic features: cap margin faintly pleated-furrowed.
