Grows singly or in small groups, only in deciduous (oak, birch, beech) communities and mixed forests. Should not be eaten because of its bitter taste. Rare. Should be classed as protected.

pilksvarude-mazaspore.habitat: Cones of coniferous trees (spruce, pine, larch)
pilksvarude-mazaspore.features: Spores tiny, gills very crowded, narrow
desc: Fruiting bodies tiny. Cap 1-2 cm across, flattened, with an inconspicuous blunt umbo, surface smooth, matt, pale brown, yellowish-brown, the margin paler. Gills very crowded, narrow, thin, adnexed, brownish, yellowish-brownish. Stem 1-4x0.1-0.2 cm, greyish-brown, brownish, grey-frosted, dotted. Flesh thin, tough, without any particular smell or taste. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies yellowish-brown, growing only on pine and spruce cones. Appears as a dozen or so fruiting bodies, in small groups. Very common. Saprotroph. Its relative, Baeospora myriadophylla (B. myriadophylla), also grows in our forests; it is somewhat larger and has been found only once (Kėdainiai district, Lančiūnava forests). Inedible.

pilksvarude-salmabude.habitat: On the bark of living deciduous trees and on snags, windfalls
pilksvarude-salmabude.features: Gills distant, with a pink tinge
desc: Fruiting bodies tiny. Cap 0.3-1 cm across, convex, bluntly flattened, matt, translucent, dirty reddish-brown, the margin paler, furrowed. Gills distant, narrow, whitish, with a pink tinge, adnate. Stem 0.3-1.3 cm long and 0.2-0.5 cm thick, dark reddish-brown. Flesh thin, the colour of the cap. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies dark reddish-brown, delicate. Grows on the bark of living deciduous trees, especially limes, horse chestnuts and maples, usually moss-covered. Also occurs on snags, branches and windfalls. Common. Saprotroph. Inedible.

pilksvazale-skujagalve.features: Cap and stem greyish-yellowish, ivory-coloured, gills brown
desc: Fruiting bodies 2-6 cm across. Cap convex, later flattened, with or sometimes without an umbo, greyish-greenish, greyish-yellowish. Young gills greyish-yellowish, later yellowish-brown, adnate. Stem 3-8x0.3-0.8 cm, firm, the colour of the cap. Flesh thin, greyish, without any particular smell or taste. Characteristic features: grows on deciduous wood, in groups, sometimes large ones. Appears on rotten deciduous wood, its debris and sawdust. Inedible. Uncommon.

platusis-ausunis.features: Upper surface of the fruiting body brown, sand-coloured, underside whitish, cream
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized, 5-10 cm across and up to 3-5 cm tall, rarely larger, like deep bowls, when mature irregularly wavy saucer-shaped, stalkless or with an inconspicuous short stem sunk in the substrate. Cap somewhat wrinkled, grey or even dark brown, the underside (of young ones) of similar colour, pale-granular, becoming paler to whitish as it grows, and especially as it dries. Flesh yellowish, fragile. Grows singly or several fruiting bodies together, on the ground, favouring humus-rich soil, sometimes even rotted wood, but also grows well in sandy places. Uncommon. Some sources state that it is edible.

plaukuotpedis-plempis.features: Stem yellow felty-hairy, fruiting bodies hardy, withstand drought
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 3-8 cm across, flattened, irregularly contorted, fibrous, as if striped, reddish-brown, greyish-brown, fading to brownish, not fleshy. Gills fairly distant, yellowish, yellowish-brown, adnate. Stem 3-8x0.3-0.7 cm, the colour of the cap, fibrous near the gills, increasingly thickening towards the base, yellowish-hairy, woolly, looking as if it had a yellow, bristly, felt-like sheath. Flesh thin, yellowish, tasteless, odourless. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies very tough, cap thin-fleshed. Grows singly or in groups, on leaves and twigs. Inedible, very common.

ploksciasis-blizgutis.habitat: On birches, more rarely on other deciduous stumps and windfalls
ploksciasis-blizgutis.features: The crust cracks audibly when pressed
desc: Fruiting bodies perennial, large, 10-40 cm across, in the form of semicircular, flat caps, solitary, often several fused together, surface uneven, wrinkled, knobbly, concentrically zoned; the crust hard, cracking audibly as it gives way when pressed, greyish-brownish, brown, greyish-chocolate; in old fungi as if floured (powdered) with fallen cocoa-coloured spores. Hymenophore surface at first white, later yellowish, pale brown, turning brown when pressed. Flesh woody, corky. Grows in forests and parks on fallen deciduous trees, snags and stumps, rarely on conifers. Causes a white or yellowish rot of the wood. Very common, a major forest sanitiser.

pluknine-sklebotinija.features: Fruiting bodies growing from a sclerotium
desc: Fruiting bodies small, long-stemmed, several growing from one sclerotium, round and closed when young, later the cap and stem develop. Cap 1–3 cm across, bowl-shaped or shaped like a wide goblet, with the margin curled up or turned out, lobed; the inside smooth, sometimes coarsely wrinkled, dark brown, yellowish-brown, the outer side ochre-yellow, pale brownish. Stem 2-8 (10) cm long and 2-3 (3) cm thick, hollow, curved, brown, thickened near the cap, of even thickness below, black in the lower part, brown felty-hairy down to the sclerotium. Flesh thin, of waxy consistency, odourless, slightly acrid-tasting. Grows from a sclerotium formed on the roots of wood anemones (Anemone), in damp, humus-rich soil. Very similar to the Pixie Cup, which appears only on bonfire sites. Inedible.

pukuotasis-nuosedis.features: Stem with a white veil-like ring zone, flesh with an unpleasant smell of radish
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 5-8 (10) cm across, flattened when mature, sometimes with a blunt umbo, yellowish-brownish, ochre-, reddish-brown, white-fibrous, scaly, when old as if cracked. Gills pale reddish-brown, rusty-brown, notched. Stem 6-12 (12)x1-2 (3) cm, thickening towards the base, white when young, covered with tufts of white veil, with a ring-like or even membranous remnant of the veil, yellowish-brown below it. Flesh brownish, firm, smelling of radish, slightly bitter-tasting. Characteristic features: brick-red gills, white-downy stem. Grows singly or in small groups, favouring the vicinity of spruce. Inedible.

Fruiting bodies medium-sized, fleshy. Cap grows up to 10 cm across, whitish with a pinkish tinge when young, older ones covered with dense, small purplish-pink scales, looking as if mottled with brownish-yellow and red spots. Gills white, old ones pinkish-brownish, red-spotted, decurrent. Stem 5-7 cm long and 1.5-2 cm thick, white near the gills, pinkish-brown below, with a pink tinge. Flesh white, brown, soft, bitter-tasting. Characteristic features: a fungus of coniferous, especially pine, forests. Very similar is the brittlegill woodwax (Hygrophorus russula (Schaeff.: Fr.) Qusl), but it is larger and grows in mixed and deciduous forests, especially in calcareous oak woods. Rare, only a few sites are known. Inedible because of its bitter taste. Warmth-loving. Protected.

purpurine-plutpinte.habitat: Forests, parks, gardens, on rotten deciduous wood
desc: Fruiting bodies spreading, with the margins detached from the substrate, or forming caps 0.5-2 cm across fused together in overlapping tiers, their upper side whitish, greyish or yellowish, softly fibrous, hairy, wrinkled. Hymenophore smooth or wrinkled, purplish-violet, of waxy, gelatinous consistency, when old brownish, dry, hard. Characteristic features: cap surface felt-like. Grows on deciduous snags, stumps, windfalls, branches and stored timber, especially firewood, also occurring on conifers. Causes a white rot of the wood. Very common. A saprotroph, a good forest sanitiser. In rare cases it acts as a weak biotroph.

pusgaubte-gleiviabude.features: Cap helmet-shaped, stem long with a delicate ring, spores large
desc: Small fruiting bodies. Cap 2-3 (3) cm across, surface smooth, slimy, yellowish-cream, straw-coloured. Gills violet-greyish-brown, adnate. Stem slender, 5-10 (15) cm long and about 0.3 cm thick, with a delicate, falling-off ring encircling the stem obliquely. Flesh yellowish, thin. Characteristic features: grows only on excrement, cap and stem yellowish.
Appears in small groups on the excrement of wild animals and domestic livestock. Inedible, very common. A sanitiser that cleans the environment. Has psychotropic properties.

pusrutuline-humarija.features: Tiny, hairy fungi, the margin fringed with eyelash-like hairs
desc: Fruiting bodies small, stalkless, 2-3 cm across, shaped like a round bowl, the margin straight or bent inwards, the upper (hymenial) side purplish-white, pearly white, later greyish-yellowish, the underside brown, with brown bristles, rough. Flesh firm, pale. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies shaped like a shallow bowl. Grows singly or in small groups, among grass, in damp places, on humus-rich soil and rotten organic debris. Not rare.

pustasis-gniauztenis.habitat: Sandy pine forests, especially burnt areas
pustasis-gniauztenis.features: Irregularly shaped, spreading, chocolate-coloured fruiting bodies
desc: Strange, stalkless fruiting bodies, 3-10 (13) cm in size, when young like conical bumps, later spreading out, wavy-knobbly, reddish-brown, brown, chocolate-coloured or even brownish-black. Instead of a stem there are only thickened mycelial cords or rhizoids, penetrating the substrate like roots. Flesh yellowish, without smell or taste. Grows singly and in groups, like a large scab or a melted piece of chocolate, on pine roots (a parasite of pines). Fairly common, edible, but of little value. Very similar are Ustulina vulgaris and Daldinia concentrica, but these fungi grow on stumps, windfalls and branches of deciduous trees and are a charred, hard mass, almost black or violet-black in colour.

raudonkraste-pintaine.habitat: On rotten coniferous and deciduous wood
raudonkraste-pintaine.features: Large woody fruiting bodies with reddish-orange margins
desc: Fruiting bodies perennial, large, hoof-shaped, 10–30 (50) cm across, usually solitary or several fused into one, attached to the substrate by the side. Surface with a hard, shiny, resinous, bare crust, furrowed by new zones added each year, pale yellowish, yellowish-orange, reddish-brown, chestnut; the margins pale yellowish, pinkish or orange, often, especially when young, with drops of liquid. Hymenophore white, cream, when old yellowish, lemon-coloured, brownish, in wet weather exuding drops of liquid. Flesh corky, smelling of musty wood and soured mushrooms. Grows in forests and parks on coniferous and deciduous snags, windfalls and stumps. Causes a brown rot. Very common, an active forest sanitiser. Of interest to physicians.

raudonkraste-salmabude.habitat: Coniferous, more rarely deciduous forests, on needles and twigs
desc: Fruiting bodies tiny. Cap 0.5-1.5 cm across, bell-shaped, later flattened, with an umbo, translucent, reddish-brown, brown, with a skin-coloured tinge, fading to cream, the margin furrowed. Gills narrow, distant, greyish, adnate, edges reddish-brown. Stem 3-7 (10) cm long and 0.5-1 cm thick, grey near the gills, ochre-pink below, the colour of the cap; when broken a purple liquid flows out. Flesh thin, tough, greyish-pink, with an unpleasant smell and taste. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies ochre-pink, tiny, a purple liquid flows out when the stem is broken. Grows in small groups. Inedible. In the photo – a bleeding bonnet ravaged by the mould Rizopus nigricans Ehrenb.

raudonsulte-salmabude.habitat: Rotten deciduous wood, most often of black or grey alder
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 1–3 cm across, bell-shaped, when old flattened-convex, with an umbo, conical, the margin furrowed, fringed, purplish-brown, rusty-brown. Gills distant, white, adnate; when broken, droplets of reddish-brown liquid ooze out, leaving a brown band when they dry. Stem 3–8x0.2–0.4 cm, the colour of the cap, whitish-frosted near the gills, the base conspicuously hairy, bristly; when broken a reddish-brown liquid is released. Flesh thin, brownish, smelling of mould, rather sharp-tasting. Characteristic features: when the cap or stem is broken, droplets of reddish-brown liquid ooze out. Grows in tufts and groups on fallen alders, rarely on branches and snags of other deciduous trees. Common. Wood saprotroph. Inedible.

raukslinis-ziurytis.habitat: On rotten deciduous wood (stumps, snags, windfalls, branches)
raukslinis-ziurytis.features: Yellow, orange, curly lumps of jelly-like consistency
desc: Fruiting bodies small, 2-5 (6) cm across, round, irregularly shaped, curly, deeply wrinkled, brain-like lumps. Young ones orange-yellow, fading with age to sulphur-yellow, yellowish, whitish, of jelly-like consistency. Flesh gelatinous, later soft, and when old even deliquescent, flabby. When dried, they revive after rain or after light frosts (down to -10 C) and continue to grow. Grows in forests and parks all year round, even in winter, on felled deciduous trees, especially on aspen and birch branches, snags and windfalls. Inedible, very common.

raupletasis-vingurelis.features: Hymenophore labyrinthine, almost gill-like, turning red when pressed
desc: Fruiting bodies large, annual, 5-15 cm across, in the form of semicircular, sometimes round, fan-shaped caps attached to the substrate by the side, solitary or fused in overlapping tiers, radially wrinkled, with concentric zones, whitish, whitish-brownish, greyish-brownish.

Tubes 1-6 mm long, pores round or labyrinthine, whitish-yellowish, pale brownish-brown, often covered with a greyish bloom which takes on a pink tinge when pressed, later turning brown. Flesh yellowish, brownish, corky.
Grows in forests, parks and gardens only on dead deciduous trees, snags, stumps and branches, most widespread on willow. Causes a white rot of the wood. An active saprotroph.

rausvasis-siurpis.habitat: On deciduous trees, fallen twigs, branches, trunks
rausvasis-siurpis.features: Young fruiting bodies red, mature ones blackish-brown, round
desc: Perithecial stromata tiny, 0.5–1 cm across, round, globose, at first brownish-red, brick-red, darkening with age to brown, blackish-brown, with a tiny opening at the top for spores to escape. The inner mass blackish-brown. Characteristic features: widespread in forests, more rarely in parks, on fallen or dead branches. Grows singly but close to one another, in groups, on branches that look as if covered with small knobs. Common. An active saprotroph.

rausvasis-skiautenelis.habitat: Trunks of deciduous trees, dried-out spots
rausvasis-skiautenelis.features: No stem, cap reddish-brown, fruiting bodies tough
desc: Fruiting bodies tiny. Cap 0.5-2.5 cm across, hoof-shaped, reddish-brown, brown, white-fibrous, the margin bent downwards, furrowed. Gills distant, pinkish, edges notched, with a violet tinge, converging to one point – the place of a rudimentary stem. Flesh pale, greyish, elastic, odourless, not bitter. Characteristic features: grows on trunks of deciduous trees, especially alders and willows. Appears in small groups, late in autumn and on warm winter days. Rare. Inedible.

rausvataske-salmabude.features: Cap very fragile, with reddish-brown spots and dots
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 2-3 (4) cm across, bell-shaped-conical when young, later flattened, with an umbo, translucently furrowed, cream, whitish-cream, pink-spotted. Gills distant, thick, not narrow, greyish, pink-dotted when old, adnexed, fragile. Stem 5 - 7x0.2-0.3 cm, fragile, the colour of the cap, white-hairy at the base. Flesh white, thin, fragile, without any particular smell or taste. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies fragile, growing on fallen needles, in groups, sometimes even in colonies. Grows in coniferous forests, in places as if sown. Very common. A litter saprotroph. Inedible.

rausvoji-pintaine.habitat: Forests, parks, most often spruce forests
desc: Fruiting bodies perennial, attached to the substrate by the side singly or several together. Usually hoof-shaped, 3–8 cm across. Surface of young ones uneven, wrinkled, finely shaggy, later smooth, bare, covered with a blackish crust, blackish-pink, greyish-brown, brownish-black, the margins pointed, pink. Hymenophore pink, greyish-pink, brownish-brown. Flesh woody, hard. Grows in damp coniferous and deciduous forests on spruce windfalls and snags, also occurring on deciduous trees. In Lithuania found only on spruce. Causes a brown rot of the wood, very rare. A saprotroph of spruce.

Young fruiting bodies egg-shaped, globose, 1.8-2 cm across, white, with a greyish, yellowish, pinkish-yellowish tinge, with a slimy jelly-like layer inside. In the upper part it splits into a lobed volva, from which grows a receptacle 7-9 cm long and 1-1.8 cm thick, honeycombed, hollow, cylindrical, sometimes curved, carmine-red, blunt or pointed. Gleba dark greenish-brown, slimy, shiny, with an unpleasant smell. Very rare, protected.

rievetoji-miege.habitat: Forests, parks, gardens, among rotting wood and twigs
rievetoji-miege.features: A fungus resembling a bird's nest with eggs
desc: Fruiting bodies small, 1–1.5 cm tall and 1 cm across, elongated-ovoid, the white covering overgrown with brown felty hairs. As the fruiting body grows, its upper part widens, the covering (as in puffballs) bursts, only ragged white shreds remain at the margin, and the fruiting body takes on the form of a beautiful small goblet with regular grooves inside as if engraved, between which lens-shaped peridioles with spores lie like little coins. Grows in groups and colonies. Inedible, fairly common, a good sanitiser of the environment.

ritiniasporis-klumpiaausis.features: Differs from other oysterlings by its small cylindrical spores
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 0.5-3 cm across, horse-hoof-shaped when young, later fan-shaped, irregular, wavy-lobed, greyish, greyish-yellowish, brownish, attached to the substrate by the side; there is no stem, or only a rudimentary remnant of it. Young gills white, later yellowish-brownish, with a pink tinge. Flesh white, thin. Characteristic features: white, slightly fibrous fruiting bodies, spores small. Grows in small groups or groups, fused in overlapping tiers – cap above cap, on deciduous, rarely on dead coniferous wood. Wood saprotroph. Not rare. 150 species of Crepidotus have been described, while in Lithuania only 11 have been identified so far; all are saprotrophs, there are no edible or poisonous ones.

Fruiting bodies small. Cap 1-3 (4) cm across, convex-flattened, with or without an umbo, faintly scaly, brownish-pink, brick-red, copper-coloured. Young gills white, soon becoming brownish-pink, adnate. Stem 2-3x0.2-0.3 cm, of even thickness, brownish-pink, white-dotted near the gills, fragile. Flesh white, later pink, thin, not bitter. Characteristic features: brownish-pink fruiting bodies (cap, gills and stem). Grows singly, favouring the vicinity of black alder and willow. Very rare. Inedible. Only one site is known – in Žemaitija National Park.

rudakepure-jaunabude.habitat: Mixed and coniferous forests, shrublands, gardens
rudakepure-jaunabude.features: Cap margin with a concentric band of yellowish-brownish scales
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 3-5 cm across, rarely larger, dirty greyish-brown, the central part chocolate, darker, the margin paler, greyish-cream, fibrous, scaly. Gills greyish-brown, adnate. Stem 3-7 cm long, sometimes longer, up to 1 cm thick, brownish. Flesh brownish, thin, bitter-tasting. Characteristic features: a sharp, unpleasant aroma (of old radishes, gas). Grows in groups, favouring forest edges and grassy roadsides overgrown with shrubs. Inedible. Similar are grey, greyish-brown knights (the grey, greyish-brown and mottled knights), but they do not have such an unpleasant smell, and their gills are white, greyish, never brown.

rudasis-kiskiaausis.habitat: Coniferous forests, on rotten needles, among mosses
rudasis-kiskiaausis.features: Fruiting bodies brown, with a short greyish stem
desc: Fruiting bodies small, ear-shaped, 1.5-2.5 cm wide and up to 5 cm tall, bright yellowish-brown, reddish-brown, brown, the underside faintly granular. Stem short, fibrous, whitish. Flesh yellowish, thin, fragile. Characteristic features: favours the vicinity of spruce. Grows singly, most often several fruiting bodies together or even in small groups. Uncommon.

rudasis-zvaigzdinas.features: Exoperidium thick, reddish-brown, with a pink tinge
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. At first globose, 5-8 (10) cm across, later the exoperidium splits into 6-7 rays, sometimes more. The rays have a pink tinge, when old brown, thick, fleshy, firm, rough, encrusted with soil on the outside. The endoperidium is an ovoid or globose body, 2-3 cm across, with or without an inconspicuous opening, greyish, reddish or dark brown. Gleba dark brown. Grows in forests, singly or several fruiting bodies together.

rudoji-sakabude.features: Cap conspicuously furrowed, stem white-woolly at the base
desc: Fruiting bodies small, tiny. Cap 1.5-4 cm across, convex when young, later raised-flattened, slightly depressed, reddish-brown, chestnut-coloured, furrowed to the middle, fading with age to greyish-cream. Gills cream, old ones reddish-brown, adnate or slightly decurrent. Stem 2-5x0.2-0.5 cm, the colour of the cap, with a white coating at the base. Flesh thin, brown, fragile, without any particular smell or taste. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies reddish-brown, appearing in the second half of autumn and early in spring. Grows singly or in small groups on wood debris. Inedible. Common. Wood saprotroph.

rusvoji-tubifera.habitat: On rotten wood, leaves, forest litter
desc: Plasmodium whitish, yellowish, soon becoming dark pink, reddish-pink. Sporangia cylindrical, cigar-shaped, 3–5 mm long, tightly packed together, shiny, reddish-brown, purplish-brown, yellowish-brown, growing on a well-developed hypothallus up to 10-15 cm across. Characteristic features: sporangia cigar-shaped, red. Grows in summer and autumn on rotten wood and leaves.

rutuline-raudene.habitat: On rotting coniferous, more rarely deciduous wood
rutuline-raudene.features: Young aethalia pink, mature ones yellowish-brown
desc: Plasmodium reddish-pink. Aethalia usually globose, from the size of a pea to that of a nut (0.5–2 cm), orange-pink when young, yellowish-brown, yellowish-grey when mature, covered with reddish-brown warts; the inner mass liquid, soft, pink, when old hardening, turning grey and developing into spores. Spores 5-7 pm. Characteristic features: the most widespread slime mould, the colour of whose aethalia varies greatly. Grows singly or in groups. Very common in forests, parks, gardens and homesteads.

saknine-pintene.habitat: On conifers, most often on spruce roots, stumps, windfalls
saknine-pintene.features: Widespread at the root bases of spruces, more rarely pines
desc: Fruiting bodies annual or perennial, 5-20 cm across, of irregular shape, solitary or arranged in overlapping tiers, spreading, with the margins raised from the substrate, or in the form of flat caps attached to the substrate by the side; surface uneven, concentrically furrowed, from yellowish-brown to dark blackish-brown, the margins paler. Hymenophore white, when old yellowish, cream, brownish. Flesh corky, yellowish, with a faint mushroom smell. Grows in forests on roots, snags, stumps and windfalls of spruces, pines and other conifers, also occurring on deciduous trees.
Causes a white mottled rot of the roots and butt; a dangerous parasite, especially of spruces.

sakniskoji-jaunabude.habitat: On roots of oak, lime, ash, hazel or birch
sakniskoji-jaunabude.features: Fruiting bodies yellow, smelling of almonds
desc: Fruiting bodies medium to large. Cap 5-10 (12) cm across, raised-flattened when mature, slimy, glossy when dry, fleshy, fibrous, scaly, ochre, reddish-brown, fading to yellowish, brownish. Gills whitish, cream, old ones reddish-brown, notched. Stem 4–12 (15–20)x1–3 cm, spindle-shaped, tapering like a root, with a conspicuous membranous ring, below the ring the stem is yellow-scaly, firm, tough. Flesh whitish, thick, smelling of almonds, slightly bitter-tasting. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies yellowish-brown, scaly, stem tapering like a root, with a long rhizoid-like extension. Grows mostly in deciduous, more rarely mixed forests. Inedible. Rare.

From a shiny, icicle-shaped or white plasmodium grow vertical, straight, usually branched, shiny, translucent, white, yellowish sporangia 0.5-1 cm long and 0.5-1 mm thick. Characteristic features: one of the most beautiful slime moulds, like a delicate coral. Grows on rotting and rotten wood, rarely on rotting leaves and forest litter. Not rare.

samanine-kugiabude.habitat: Among mosses and on moss-covered stumps, windfalls, snags
samanine-kugiabude.features: Fruiting bodies delicate, fragile, yellow, brownish-yellow
desc: Fruiting bodies tiny. Cap 0.3-1.5 cm across, bluntly bell-shaped, finally convex, shiny, translucent, furrowed, delicate, fragile. Gills creamy yellow, adnate, narrow, distant, adnexed or adnate. Stem 2-5x0.1 cm. Flesh very thin, without any particular or with a very faint smell of flour, not bitter. Characteristic features: tiny fruiting bodies glowing yellow among mosses like little candles. Grows singly or in small groups. Saprotroph, the most widespread of all Galerina species in forests and bogs. 200 species have been described; in Lithuania 27 species have been found so far, saprophytes of wood, soil and herbaceous plants, inedible, and 2 are deadly poisonous.

seriuotasis-skylenis.features: Large, blackish-brown fruiting bodies, surface rough, felty
desc: Fruiting bodies annual, large, 10-30 cm across and larger, semicircular, hoof-shaped, attached to the substrate by the broad side, surface coarsely bristly, hairy, felty, unzoned, lumpy, reddish-yellowish-brown, when old blackish-brown. Pores yellow, turning black when touched, young ones exude sticky droplets of liquid. Flesh yellow, watery when young, corky and hard when old. Grows singly or several fruiting bodies together on deciduous trees, most often fruit trees, especially walnuts and apple trees. Causes a white rot of the wood. A parasite. Very rare.

siaurinis-dyglenis.habitat: On maples, oaks, poplars, at damaged spots on trees
desc: Fruiting bodies large, up to 30 cm across, made up of fused flat lobes arranged in overlapping tiers one above another, attached to the substrate by one edge; surface whitish, later becoming yellowish, in old ones yellowish-brown, hairy. The spines on the underside yellowish, up to 1.3 (2) cm long. Flesh white, firm, 2–4 cm thick, slightly bitter-tasting. Characteristic features: grows only on deciduous trees, at a damaged spot, of soft, corky consistency, easily recognised. Causes a white rot of the wood. Not rare. A fungus of parks and avenues, causing considerable damage to trees, especially maples.

Fruiting bodies large, annual, 5-15 cm across, fan-shaped, semicircular, attached to the substrate by the broad edge, usually fused in overlapping tiers, watery, soft, fleshy, tough, white, cream, brown-spotted, yellowish and fibrous when dried. Hymenophore white, yellowish, pores round or angular. Flesh white, soft, with an unpleasant smell and a sour-bitter taste. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies whitish, brown-spotted, bitter-tasting. Grows in forests and parks on fallen spruces, sometimes on pine stumps, rarely on living trees. Causes a brownish rot of the wood. Uncommon. A destroyer of wood, mostly a saprotroph.

sieraspalve-skujagalve.habitat: On rotten coniferous wood, stumps, windfalls, snags
sieraspalve-skujagalve.features: The predominant colour of the fruiting body is greenish-yellow, sulphur-yellow
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 3-6 cm across, conical, later raised-flattened, flattened, with an umbo, greenish-yellow, sulphur-yellow, the margin paler, bent downwards. Gills yellowish, later sulphur-yellow, old ones yellowish-brown. Stem 3-9 (12)x0.5-1.5 cm, thickening towards the base, the colour of the cap when young, reddish-brown when old, fibrous. Flesh sulphur-yellow, soft, without any particular smell, not bitter. Characteristic features: gills from sulphur-yellow to yellowish-brown. Grows in small groups on dead conifers, in forests, more rarely in parks. Inedible, not rare. In Lithuania 20 species of Pholiota are found, almost all of them wood saprotrophs and forest sanitisers; several species are edible but of little value, and there are no poisonous ones.

siukscioji-kempe.features: Surface of the fruiting body zoned, hairy
desc: Fruiting bodies annual, in the form of semicircular caps, solitary, more rarely several fused together in overlapping tiers one above another, attached to the tree bark by the edge, 3–10 cm across, up to 1 cm thick. Surface covered with dense, glossy hairs, zoned, whitish, yellowish, yellowish-brownish. Hymenophore smooth, white, yellowish, grey, pores round. There are no cystidia; the hyphal system is trimitic. Characteristic features: grows only on dead deciduous, very rarely coniferous wood. Grows on birches, hazels, limes, aspens, willows, plums, apple trees, cherries, etc., also occurring on windfalls, snags, branches and stumps of pines and spruces; causes a white rot of the wood. Very common. Also fairly common in gardens on half-dead and dead plums, more rarely apple and pear trees.

siurksciakote-smirdekle.features: Stem black, rough, granular, yellowish at the top, stinking
desc: Fruiting bodies tiny. Cap 0.5-1.5 cm across, flattened, wrinkled, depressed in the middle, the margin furrowed, tough, thin, reddish-brown, brownish. Gills narrow, distant, semi-decurrent or not even reaching the stem. Stem thread-like, up to 3 cm long, matt, rough, fibrous-granular, as if frosted, brownish-black, yellowish near the gills. Flesh membranous, thin, tough, with an unpleasant stinking smell, especially when rubbed between the fingers. Characteristic features: tiny, stinking fungi growing on fallen needles. Grows singly, but sometimes as if sown – close to one another, on spruce and pine needles, hundreds of fruiting bodies. Very common. A saprotroph of needles.

siurksciakotis-plempis.features: Stem dotted, warty, fruiting bodies tough, growing in tufts
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 1–3 (3) cm across, thin, tough, yellowish-brownish. Gills very narrow, crowded, yellowish, whitish, adnate. Stem 3–10x0.3–0.6 cm, cartilaginous, round, flaky, covered with tiny warts, greyish. Flesh thin, tough, without any particular smell or taste. Characteristic features: gills very narrow, crowded. Grows in grassy places and thickets. Appears in groups, the fruiting bodies often stuck together in tufts of a dozen or more or even several dozen; inedible, very common.

siurkscioji-trapiabude.habitat: Roadsides, forest edges, parks, ditch banks
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 3-9 (10) cm across, flattened, with a blunt umbo, dirty yellowish-brown, orange-brown, fading to brownish, shaggy with reddish fibrils. Gills cream, later reddish-brown, chocolate-coloured when old, adnate. Stem 3–10x0.3–1.3 cm, not fragile, yellowish, brownish, white-dotted in the upper part. Flesh yellowish, fairly thick, without any particular smell or taste. Characteristic features: widespread along ditches, roadsides, forest edges, among grass. Grows in groups, among grass, in damp places, most often near drainage ditches. Some sources state that it is edible though of little value, others that it is inedible or even poisonous. Common.

skydeline-blakstienute.features: This eyelash cup stands out from many others by its long hairs
desc: Fruiting bodies tiny, 0.3-1.2 cm across, stalkless, saucer- or shallow disc-shaped, orange-red, pinkish-red, the margin covered with long blackish bristles, the very edge in particular fringed like eyelashes. Flesh thin, pinkish. Characteristic features: small, orange-red fruiting bodies. Grows singly or in groups, on the ground, on plant debris, sometimes on bonfire sites. Common.

Fruiting bodies medium-sized and larger. Cap grows up to 10 cm across, fibrous, scaly, yellowish-brown. Gills greenish-yellow, broadly adnate. Stem up to 8 cm long and 1 cm thick, yellow near the gills, greyish-brownish below, covered with white mycelial fluff at the base, without a ring. Flesh yellow, very bitter, with an unpleasant smell. Characteristic features: the fungus tastes very bitter when chewed. Grows only on dead pine and spruce wood. Appears in small groups. Very common. Inedible. About 10 species of Gymnopilus grow in Lithuania; because of their bitter taste all are inedible, and some are even mildly poisonous. Honey fungi are not bitter, their caps are more or less scaly, their stems have rings and are fibrous; they do not resemble rustgills.

spindulinis-skylenis.habitat: On alder snags, sometimes also on other deciduous trees
spindulinis-skylenis.features: Brownish-yellow fruiting bodies, surface rough, fibrous
desc: An annual fungus. Fruiting bodies 2–8 cm across, in the form of semicircular caps attached to the tree trunk by the side, arranged in overlapping tiers, fused together at the sides, stretching in rows. Cap surface wrinkled, yellowish or reddish, even blackish-brown. Pores of even size, silvery, so that depending on the distance they shimmer and radiate, changing colour. Flesh corky, hard, yellowish-brown. Hymenophore whitish, greyish, turning brownish when touched. Characteristic features: a chain of caps stretches over an area 1-3 m long on the tree trunk, the pores shimmer, changing their lustre. Grows in forests, parks and bogs. Common, a good forest sanitiser.

sveinico-rudapinte.habitat: Coniferous forests, on roots of pines, spruces, larches
sveinico-rudapinte.features: Surface of the fruiting body bristly, felty, chestnut-coloured
desc: Fruiting bodies annual, large, in the form of round or semicircular, fan-shaped, fleshy caps, solitary or several fused together; surface felty, bristly, uneven, furrowed, faintly zoned, yellowish-brown, brown, chestnut-coloured. Tubes 2-7 (10) mm long, pores round, angular, elongated, brownish, pale brown, tobacco-coloured. Flesh soft, watery, orange, yellowish-brown.
Characteristic features: fruiting bodies soft, yellow, yellowish-brown, the tubes turn brown and darken when pressed.
Grows in forests and parks at the root bases of conifers, more rarely on their stumps and windfalls. Causes a brown rot of the wood. Biotroph, saprotroph. Protected.

tabokinis-siurkstenis.habitat: On fallen deciduous, rarely coniferous branches and trunks
desc: Annual, biennial. Fruiting bodies spreading, at first round, later several fuse together to form a large garland of fruiting bodies up to 1 m long and more, with small, fragile, yellowish-brown caps detached from the substrate, their surface wrinkled and zoned. Hymenophore smooth, radially cracked, with a pink tinge, later tobacco-coloured. Grows on dead, fallen branches and snags of hazel and willow, less often of other deciduous trees. A good forest sanitiser. Very common. The similar Hymenochaete rubiginosa (H. rubiginosa) is rarer; its fruiting bodies are perennial. Both these Hymenochaete species are active saprotrophs that quickly break down fallen branches.

tamprioji-salmabude.habitat: Forests, parks, on rotten leaves, needles, twigs
tamprioji-salmabude.features: Grows late in autumn. Cap and stem slimy
desc: Fruiting bodies tiny. Cap 0.5-2 cm across, bell-shaped, when old almost flattened, with an umbo, slimy, the cuticle elastic, easily peeled, whitish-cream, lemon-yellow or even greyish-brownish. Gills white, yellowish, sticky, elastic, adnate. Stem 5-10x0.1-0.3 cm, lemon-yellow when young, later whitish-yellow, sheathed in a thick layer of slime. Flesh thin, tough, smelling of flour and grass, not bitter. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies tough, lemon-, whitish-yellow. Grows singly or several fruiting bodies together. Common. A litter saprotroph. Inedible. In Lithuania 56 species of Mycena have been recorded: saprotrophs of forest litter and wood, active decomposers of lignin and cellulose, fairly important in the life of the forest.

taurinis-zvakidelis.features: Grows on rotten wood, most often of aspen
desc: Fruiting body 3–13 cm tall, with richly branched upright branchlets growing from a thick central stem, each ending at the tip in a neat toothed little cup, as if for holding a miniature candle. Young ones pale yellow, old ones brown, sometimes even with a greyish, violet tinge. Flesh bitter-tasting. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies regularly branched, the tips of the branchlets as if capped with a miniature toothed cup. Grows in forests and parks on aspen, birch, willow, rarely on coniferous wood, sometimes in colonies. Inedible because of its bitterness, common.

tikrasis-gelsvunis.habitat: Forest edges, parks, meadows, pastures, gardens
tikrasis-gelsvunis.features: Straw-yellow, fading to yellowish, spores large
desc: Fruiting bodies small, delicate. Cap 2-5 (6) cm across, delicate, bell-shaped, later raised-flattened, with a distinct umbo, sticky, lemon-yellow, creamy yellow, fading to yellowish, the margin furrowed. Gills yellowish, old ones ochre-yellow, narrow, free. Stem 5-8 (12)x0.2-0.6 cm, thickening towards the base, the colour of the cap, fibrous, fragile. Flesh thin, yellowish, without any particular smell or taste.
Characteristic features: delicate, yellow fruiting bodies growing in meadows.
Grows singly or in small groups on humus-rich substrate. Saprotroph. Not rare. Inedible.

tikrinis-blizgutis.features: Fruiting bodies shiny, as if varnished
desc: A rather beautiful and interesting bracket. Fruiting bodies annual, in the form of round, semicircular or fan-shaped caps attached to the substrate by a lateral or eccentric stem, 5 - 20 cm across. Surface of the cap and stem yellowish-red, chestnut-coloured, shiny, as if varnished. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies reddish-brown, usually with a long stem. Grows most often on black alder and spruce stumps. Not rare. Causes a white rot of the wood. In Japan this fungus is known as „Reishi“ and in China as „Ling-zhi“; it is used in medicine. Protected.

tikroji-pintis.features: Fruiting bodies large, most often growing on birches, spores large
desc: A perennial fungus. Fruiting bodies hoof- or fan-shaped, up to 30 cm across, attached to the tree trunk by the side, hard, woody, surface leathery, smooth, whitish-grey, blackish-grey, greyish-brownish, zoned, the margins of paler shades. Flesh hard, corky, brown. Grows in deciduous and mixed forests and parks on dead deciduous trees, most often on birches (sometimes there are 10–20 fruiting bodies on a windfall or snag). Causes a white rot of the wood. Very common. In folk medicine, powder of the willow bracket and the tinder fungus was used to stop bleeding and to treat wounds.

tikroji-raudonpinte.habitat: On dead deciduous trees, especially birches, very rarely on conifers
desc: An annual fungus. Fruiting body medium-sized, up to 8 cm across, corky, flexible, fleshy; surface finely fibrous, later smooth or wrinkled, pale orange, reddish-orange, cinnabar-coloured. Hymenophore reddish-orange. Flesh soft, spongy, the colour of the cap. Characteristic features: grows mostly only on fallen birches, several fruiting bodies together, almost all year round. Grows singly or several fruiting bodies together, causing a white rot of the wood. Not only a forest sanitiser but also a showy fungus, listed in the Red Data Book of Lithuania.

trapioji-postija.features: Fruiting bodies white, turning brown when pressed or cut
desc: Fruiting bodies annual, medium-sized, in the form of caps arranged in overlapping tiers, attached to the substrate by the side. Caps 3-8 (10) cm long, 2-6 cm wide, 1-2 cm thick, flattened, surface finely wrinkled, radially furrowed, downy, white, whitish, turning brown when pressed, when old yellowish-cream, pale brown. Hymenophore white, whitish, turning brown when pressed. Tubes 0.3–1 cm long, whitish. Flesh fleshy, fibrous, white, turning brown when pressed or with age, mild-tasting. Grows in forests and parks on rotten coniferous wood – snags, stumps, windfalls. Causes an active brown rot of the wood. Common. An active saprotroph.

tusciaviduris-zvaigzdinas.habitat: Deciduous forests, parks, under spruces, on rotten needles
tusciaviduris-zvaigzdinas.features: Fruiting body most often with 8 rays
desc: Fruiting bodies globose, about 2–3 cm, when old they split and expand to 4–8 cm across, ochre, yellowish-brown. The exoperidium is leathery, firm, splitting from the top to halfway into 6-8 rays, which curl downwards like legs and form a shallow bowl holding the endoperidium, a round body 1–2 cm across with an opening at the top for scattering spores. Grows in coniferous and deciduous forests, parks, and in gardens under lilacs, favouring calcareous soil. Common. Inedible. Interesting fungi; so far 13 species of earthstars are known in Lithuania – some like spiders ready to scuttle off, and others, on the contrary, like faded, dried, withered orchids.

vagotakote-salmabude.habitat: Roots, stumps, snags in deciduous and coniferous forests, parks
vagotakote-salmabude.features: Fruiting bodies greyish-brown, stem longitudinally grooved
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 3-5 cm across, bell-shaped-conical, eventually flattened, with an umbo, wrinkled-furrowed, matt, brownish-grey, dark greyish-brown in the centre. Gills brownish, white, grey when mature, adnate. Stem 5-12x0.3-0.5 cm, longitudinally grooved, grey, greyish-brown, with a bluish tinge, whitish-frosted, white-mealy near the gills. Flesh thin, whitish, greyish, smelling of flour and wood, not bitter. Characteristic features: cap pleated-furrowed, stem long, usually grows singly. Appears singly or several fruiting bodies together. Inedible, not rare.

Fruiting bodies rather stout, large. Cap grows up to 15 (18) cm across, fleshy, greyish-brownish, yellowish-brownish, with a blunt umbo. Gills whitish, cream, adnate. Stem 5-12x1–2.5 cm, longitudinally furrowed. Flesh whitish, with an unpleasant smell and taste. Characteristic features: large fruiting bodies, an especially long stem, cap fleshy, spores amyloid. Grows several fruiting bodies together or in small groups, among grass, in forests and on roadsides. Inedible.

varpeline-sausabude.habitat: Mossy pine and spruce stumps, windfalls, snags
varpeline-sausabude.features: Cap depressed in the centre, gills decurrent
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 0.5-2 cm across, bell-shaped when young, later semi-convex, convex, the centre depressed, hygrophanous, sticky, dry, the margin conspicuously furrowed, yellowish-brown, orange-yellow, fading to yellowish. Gills yellowish, far decurrent. Stem 1-3x0.1-0.2 cm, tough, the base sometimes thickened, the colour of the cap, yellow-fibrous. Flesh thin, yellowish. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies tiny, growing in colonies. Grows in summer and autumn, mostly on mossy spruce and pine stumps, snags and windfalls. Saprotroph. Very common. Inedible.

veduokline-meskaite.habitat: Rotten spruce, pine and deciduous (hornbeam, oak) wood
veduokline-meskaite.season: Spring, autumn, even winter (in cellars, greenhouses)
desc: Fruiting bodies small to medium-sized. Cap 3-8 cm across, shell-, fan- or kidney-shaped, velvety, strongly hairy, tough, yellowish, orange-yellow. Gills the colour of the cap. There is no stem. Flesh yellow, tough, with an unpleasant smell, not bitter. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies tough, stemless, orange, spores tiny. Grows in forests and in enclosed premises on rotten coniferous, more rarely deciduous wood. Inedible, uncommon. It differs from the oyster rollrim by its stemless, hairier, fibrous orange cap.

veduokline-meskute.features: Cap fan-shaped, spores almost round, small
desc: Fruiting bodies small to medium-sized. Cap 2-8 cm across, fan-shaped, in young fruiting bodies rolled inwards, in old ones the margin bent downwards, yellowish, brownish-yellowish, sometimes with a violet or greenish tinge, fibrous-velvety. Young gills white, later the colour of the cap, with transverse cross-veins. Stem short, lateral, sometimes absent, the colour of the cap. Flesh yellowish, soft, with a pleasant smell, not bitter. Characteristic features: cap softly velvety, tough. Grows several fruiting bodies together, most often on pine wooden structures (benches, gazebos) in parks, gardens and farm buildings. An active wood destroyer.

velyvasis-plempis.habitat: Coniferous forests, especially pine, more rarely spruce and larch forests
velyvasis-plempis.features: A late-autumn, post-frost fungus, especially common in pine forests
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 2-3 cm across, bell-shaped when young, flattened when old, delicate, furrowed, reddish-, yellowish-brown, sticky. Gills brownish, thin, narrow, cream, yellowish-brownish, adnate. Stem 2-6x0.2-0.4 cm, of even thickness or thicker towards the base, yellowish-brownish. Flesh fairly thick, brownish, without smell and without taste. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies tough, yellowish-brown, small, cap furrowed. Grows singly or in small groups in coniferous forests, on and among fallen needles. Inedible. A common late-autumn fungus of pine forests.

violetine-gijabude.habitat: Living and dead deciduous wood, most often black alder, oak
violetine-gijabude.features: Most often grows in nettle-rich black-alder woods and bogs
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 2-5 cm across, conical when young, later raised-flattened, slightly depressed in the middle, fibrous, scaly, bluish-violet, becoming paler with age to greyish-brownish-violet. Gills violet-blue, taking on a brown tinge with age, adnate. Stem 2-5 (7)x0.2-0.5 cm, violet-blue. Flesh thin, the colour of the cap, rather sharp-tasting. Characteristic features: bluish-violet fruiting bodies growing on rotten wood. Appears singly or several fruiting bodies together on dead or living wood of black alder, rowan, oak and ash, in nettle-rich black-alder woods. Uncommon. Inedible.

zalingasis-trobagrybis.habitat: On dead wood, most often indoors
zalingasis-trobagrybis.features: Young fungus white, when mature turning brown, spores large
desc: Fruiting bodies large, spreading up to 50 cm across, 4 cm thick, weakly attached to the substrate, peeling off easily; young ones white, in old ones the centre turns brown while the margins stay white longer, but eventually they too turn brown. Hymenophore wrinkled, with large net-like folds, coarsely porous, yellowish-ochre, dark brown, violet-brown, usually with droplets of brown liquid. The most dangerous destroyer of wood in unventilated, enclosed premises, destroying floors, walls and windowsills, ruining houses and harming human health. It dislikes drought, sun, draughts and well-impregnated wood.

zemiakvapis-nuosedis.features: Stem without a bulb at the base, flesh with a smell of musty earth
desc: Fruiting bodies large. Cap 5-15 cm across, massive, flattened, densely and coarsely fibrous, slimy when young, especially the violet margin, violet, soon ochre-, reddish-, greyish-brown. Young gills greyish-violet, old ones reddish-brown, adnate. Stem 5-12x1.5-3 cm, thickening towards the base, ending in a semi-rounded bulb up to 4 cm across. Flesh whitish, with an unpleasant earthy smell, rather sharp-tasting. Characteristic features: massive fruiting bodies, young ones with a violet tinge. Grows in small groups in coniferous and mixed forests, favouring the vicinity of spruce. In some literature it is given as a tasty edible fungus, elsewhere as an inedible one.

ziediskasis-karpininkas.features: Fruiting bodies chocolate-coloured, cracked and whitish in the upper part
desc: Fruiting bodies branched, soft, 2-3 (5) cm tall, with a short stem thickened at the base and covered with brown fibres; from pale to dark brown, the tips of the branchlets paler – almost white, whitish; the branchlets of unequal size, flat, cracked and split in the upper part, resembling beautiful petals. Hymenophore smooth, covering the surface of all the branchlets, dark grey, greyish-brown, brown, chocolate-coloured, sometimes with a violet tinge. Grows in forests and parks, singly or in small groups on the ground. Uncommon. A litter saprotroph.

zieduotoji-kartekle.features: Cap with a pinkish tinge, spotted greenish, bitter
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 2-6 cm across, raised-flattened, with an umbo, pinkish-brown, finely scaly, spotted greenish. Gills reddish-brown, broad, edges paler, semi-decurrent. Stem 3-5x0.5-1 cm, of even thickness, reddish-brown, with a conspicuous remnant of a whitish ring. Flesh yellow, with a mild smell of wood, bitter-tasting. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies smaller than those of the large rustgill, and the stem only with a ring remnant. Grows several fruiting bodies together. Inedible, rare.

zieduotoji-mesliuke.features: Stem with a ring, spores large, black
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap grows up to 7 cm across, conical, bell-shaped, greyish-cream, cream, surface smooth or slightly cracked. Young gills greyish, old ones almost black, edges white-dotted. Stem 4-12 (15)x0.5–1 cm, with a ring, above which it is white-dotted, below greyish-brownish. Flesh whitish, mild-tasting, odourless. Characteristic features: cap cream-coloured, stem with a ring. Grows singly, rarely in small groups, on rotted sheep, cow, horse and wild boar dung. Rare, inedible. It has psychotropic properties and is therefore of interest to physicians.

zieduotoji-sakabude.features: Fruiting bodies chestnut-coloured, stem with a ring
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 3-6 cm across, irregularly flattened, chestnut-coloured, dark reddish-brown, the margin furrowed, fibrous, fading to yellowish-brownish. Gills yellowish-brown, old ones dark brownish-brown, adnate. Stem 3-10x0.3-0.6 cm, with a conspicuous, leathery, whitish ring, the colour of the cap, white-fibrous. Flesh brownish, without any particular smell or taste. Characteristic features: cap fading to yellowish-brownish, particularly fond of dead willow, alder and birch. Grows several fruiting bodies together on rotten deciduous wood (snags, windfalls). Inedible. Rare. Classed as deserving protection.

ziemine-skyletbude.features: Fruiting bodies small, hard, woody, spores small
desc: Fruiting bodies small, annual. Cap 2-5 (8) cm across, flat, sometimes with a blunt umbo or slightly depressed, matt, fibrous, finely scaly, grey, greyish-yellowish-brownish, blackish-brown when old. Tubes 1-3 pm long, whitish, pale cream or even ochre, with a white bloom, somewhat decurrent down the stem. Stem 3–6x0.2–0.5 cm, round, brownish, yellowish-brownish, finely scaly when young, smooth-surfaced when old. Flesh white, leathery, hard, without any particular smell or taste.

Characteristic features: cap finely scaly, greyish-yellowish-brownish. Grows throughout the growing season, more in spring, singly or in small groups, causing a white rot of the wood. Inedible. Common.

zieminis-karpininkas.habitat: Coniferous, deciduous and mixed forests, parks
desc: Fruiting bodies small, soft, 2-5 cm wide and tall, usually several fused together to form a rosette, also growing singly. Cap fibrous-scaly, hairy, from pale to dark brown, darkening to black when old, with paler margins. Hymenophore smooth, slightly warty, greyish-brown. Grows in larger or smaller groups in forests, from early spring to late autumn, sometimes even in winter, on fallen leaves, needles, twigs and wood chips. Especially dangerous when it establishes itself in tree nurseries, causing great losses to pine plantations. Common. Inedible.

zieminis-vertinis.season: Almost all year round, especially late autumn and mild winters
zieminis-vertinis.features: Dry, hard fruiting bodies, stem with a bulb at the base
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Globose when young, 3-6 cm tall when mature. Head 0.5-1 (1.5) cm across, round or flattened, sometimes onion-shaped, with an opening at the top, pale brown, ochre, brown, sand-coloured. Stem 1.5-6 cm long and 0.2-0.3 cm thick, fibrous, finely scaly, flaky, hollow, the colour of the cap, with a bulb at the base. Grows singly, rarely several fruiting bodies together, among grass, favouring calcareous, stony, sandy soil. Rare.

ziemkente-sausapinte.habitat: Dry, sandy pine forests, forest clearings, on the ground
ziemkente-sausapinte.features: Stem central, eccentric, sometimes several fused together
desc: Fruiting bodies annual, medium-sized. Cap 3-8 cm across, flattened, somewhat depressed, velvety, when old smooth, zoned, ochre, greyish-brown, yellowish-brown, chestnut-coloured, fading. Tubes 0.5–3 pm long, pores roundly angular, with a greyish bloom, decurrent down the stem. Stem 2–4x0.2–0.5 cm, the colour of the cap, likewise shaggy. Flesh thin, corky, tough, yellowish.
Characteristic features: fruiting bodies yellowish-brown, cap shaped like a flat-centred goblet, zoned.
Grows singly or in small groups, especially in dry pine forests. Inedible, has medicinal properties. Fairly common. Sometimes survives for two years.

zievine-salmabude.habitat: On the bark of living deciduous trees, especially limes
desc: Fruiting bodies tiny. Cap 0.3-1 cm across, convex, bluntly flattened, matt, dirty reddish-brown, the margin paler, furrowed. Gills distant, narrow, whitish, with a pink tinge, adnate. Stem 0.3-1.3 cm long and 0.2-0.5 cm thick, dark reddish-brown. Flesh thin, the colour of the cap. Characteristic features: dark reddish-brown fruiting bodies, spores round. Grows only on the bark of living deciduous trees, especially limes, horse chestnuts and maples. Common, noticed especially often in towns (squares, parks). Inedible.

zvynuotasis-dantunis.habitat: On dead, more rarely living coniferous trees
zvynuotasis-dantunis.features: Gill edges toothed, spores non-amyloid, large
desc: Fruiting bodies large. Cap 5–23 cm across, flattened, slightly depressed, scaly, cracked, fissured, white, firm. Gills crowded, broad (up to 2 cm), cream, edges toothed, semi-decurrent. Stem central, sometimes lateral, woody, white, with remnants of a ring, 5–8x2–6 cm. Flesh white, hard, firm, woody, up to 2 cm thick, with a pleasant smell, not bitter. Characteristic features: white, large, woody fruiting bodies. Cap surface cracked. Grows singly on wooden structures, most often on railway sleepers or the foundations of other buildings. Inedible. A wood saprotroph, fairly active.

aitrusis-baltikas.features: Cap greyish-brownish, with a violet tinge
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 3–8 cm across, conical when young, later flattened, with an umbo, fibrous, scaly, finely cracked in dry weather, dark grey, greyish-brownish, with a violet tinge. Gills crowded, greyish, adnate. Stem 3-8 (11)x0.5-2 cm, white, grey, sometimes with a brownish tinge, fibrous near the gills, smooth below. Flesh greyish, firm, with an unpleasant smell and bitter taste. Characteristic features: grows singly or in small groups and only in deciduous forests.
Inedible, mildly poisonous. Rare.

arsioji-tauriabude.habitat: Mixed, coniferous and deciduous forests, thickets, among grass
arsioji-tauriabude.features: Cap flattened, with a grey, white bloom, as if mealy
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 3-6 cm across, raised-flattened or even slightly depressed, matt, with a greyish bloom, whitish, greyish-yellowish, concentrically cracked. Gills narrow, crowded, greyish-yellowish, adnate or slightly decurrent. Stem 2-3x0.3-0.8 cm, firm, white, brownish when old. Flesh thin, pale brownish, mild-tasting, odourless. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies greyish, greyish-yellowish, cap cracked, spores small. Grows singly or in small groups. Inedible or even mildly poisonous, as it contains muscarine. Not rare. Similar to white-coloured meadow mushrooms, but its gills are yellowish.

balsvoji-kupstabude.habitat: Forests, parks, rarely gardens, roadsides, forest edges, ditch sides
balsvoji-kupstabude.features: Fruiting bodies white, tough, gills adnate
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized, rarely large, white. Cap grows up to 9 cm across, thin-fleshed, matt, not depressed. Gills white, cream, adnate. Stem up to 12 cm long and 2 cm thick, firm, the base tapering. Flesh thin, with a rather sharp, unpleasant smell and taste. Characteristic features: grows in groups among grass, especially on roadsides and ditch sides; spores smooth-walled, non-amyloid, as in all Lyophyllum species. Sometimes grows in several dozen fruiting bodies. Earlier literature stated that it is edible, but recently harmful substances have been found in it and it is not recommended as food. Fairly common

baltarudis-baltikas.habitat: Pine forests, sandy places not overgrown with moss
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 5-8 (10) cm across, reddish-brown, chestnut-coloured, with blackish streaks, not fleshy. Gills white, edges brown-spotted, adnate. Stem 3- 6x0.5-1.5 cm, white. Flesh bitter-tasting, smelling of flour. Characteristic features: grows in coniferous forests, especially sandy pine forests, in groups; the cap, and sometimes the stem, very sandy. Common. Mildly poisonous; some sources mention it as inedible.

bekvape-gijabude.features: Spores angular, with a pink tinge
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 5-8 (10-12) cm across, not fleshy, grey, ochre-greyish-brownish, fragile. Gills pink, reddish-brown, adnate. Stem 7-12x0.5-1.5 cm, white, fragile. Flesh whitish, thin, not bitter, with a faint smell of flour. Characteristic features: rather fragile fruiting bodies, gills reddish-brown, grows in damp, grassy places, in nettle beds. Grows singly, more often in groups, very widespread in our forests, woodlands and bogs. Inedible, mildly poisonous.

blyskusis-meslinukas.habitat: Forests, parks, fallow land, meadows, pastures
blyskusis-meslinukas.features: Cap surface cracked, fissured, stem of medium length
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 2-3 (3) cm across, half bell-shaped, convex-conical, finally flattened, with an umbo, smooth-surfaced when young, cracked when old, as if scaly, pale whitish, ash-coloured or pale brownish. Gills grey, black when old, broad, adnexed. Stem 3-8x0.2-0.4 cm, whitish, thickening and turning brownish towards the base. Flesh membranous, brownish, without any particular smell or taste. Characteristic features: cap pale brownish-grey, spores large, black, lemon-shaped. Grows on the excrement of wild animals, singly or in small groups. Not rare. Has psychotropic properties causing hallucinations; of interest to physicians.

Fruiting bodies small. Cap 1–5 cm across, hemispherical, later bluntly convex, finally flattened, with an inconspicuous raised area in the middle, matt, yellowish-, greenish-reddish or brown, finely fibrous or even scaly. Gills crowded, orange, brownish-orange, adnate. Stem 3-6 (8)x0.3-0.8 cm, of even thickness, sometimes tapering at the base, soft yellow, yellowish-brown, fibrous. Flesh thin, yellowish, greenish-yellow, with an unpleasant smell of radish, slightly bitter. Characteristic features: young gills orange, old ones brownish-orange. Grows in groups in coniferous, rarely deciduous forests. Poisonous, very common.

didysis-bobausis.features: Differs from the false morel by its larger fruiting bodies and spores
desc: Fruiting bodies large. Cap 8-12 cm across, of irregular shape, surface wrinkled, yellowish-brown, yellowish-ochre or yellowish-brown, the margins free or fused with the stem. Stem 3–8x4–8 cm, hollow, wrinkled, finely granular, whitish, pale yellowish, yellowish-brown. Flesh yellowish, fragile, with a pleasant smell and taste. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies massive, cap more yellow, stem thick. Grows on the ground and on decayed wood. Poisonous when fresh, like the false morel. Not rare. Most often these two Gyromitra species are confused and not distinguished.

didzioji-kartekle.habitat: On rotten deciduous wood, especially birch, black alder
didzioji-kartekle.features: The largest rustgill, fruiting bodies yellowish-brown
desc: Fruiting bodies large. Cap 5-15 cm across, massive, fleshy, flattened when mature, sometimes even depressed, surface slightly velvety, scaly, yellowish-orange, yellowish-brown. Gills yellowish, later ochre-yellow, reddish-brown, crowded, thick, adnexed. Stem 5-15 (20)x1-3 (4) cm, of even thickness near the gills, thickened in the middle, tapering at the base, with a broad, yellow, membranous ring. Flesh thick, firm, sulphur-yellow, with a persistent smell, bitter. Characteristic features: stem with a conspicuous ring, spores granular. Grows several fruiting bodies together, rarely in groups, on deciduous windfalls, stumps and snags. Poisonous, rare. Has hallucinogenic properties. Do not confuse it with honey fungi

dryzuotasis-baltikas.habitat: Coniferous forests, more often pine forests, rarely deciduous woods
desc: Medium-sized fruiting bodies. Cap 3-8 cm across, smooth, slightly shiny, acutely conical, grey, bluish-grey, with blackish streaks, not fleshy. Gills whitish, grey, adnate. Stem 7-12x1-1.3 cm, grey, brownish. Flesh thin, whitish, odourless, with a rather sharp, burning taste. Characteristic features: cap conical, with a pointed top, stem long. Grows singly, favouring mossy pine forests. According to some authors it is poisonous, according to others inedible. Common. By its pointed conical cap and long stem it is easily distinguished from other grey knights (the greyish-brown, mottled, grey and even blackish-green knights).

egline-kugiabude.habitat: On rotten stumps, windfalls, snags, branches lying on the ground
egline-kugiabude.features: Cap yellowish-brown, not scaly, spores large, lemon-shaped
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 3–5 cm, sometimes even 8 cm across, yellowish-brown, surface smooth, not scaly. Gills ochre-yellow, yellowish-reddish-brown. Stem 3-7x0.3–0.8 cm, with a leathery ring, brownish, reddish-brown, greyish above the ring, slightly fibrous but not scaly. Flesh yellowish, thin, with an unpleasant smell and taste. Characteristic features: stem with a ring, not scaly, gills yellowish-brown, grows mostly on coniferous wood. Grows singly or in small groups. Very poisonous, widespread in Lithuania, common. When gathering honey fungi and sheathed woodtufts, let us not forget this fungus that is dangerous to health.

gelsvoji-musmire.habitat: Forests, sometimes forest edges, clear-cuts, sparse stands, brighter places
gelsvoji-musmire.features: Cap fading, scaly, volva rough, fused with the stem
desc: Fruiting bodies large. Cap 8-10 cm across and larger, flattened, pale yellowish-greenish, yellowish, sometimes even whitish, covered with irregular whitish remnants of the veil. Gills white, later yellowish, broad, crowded, free. Stem 8-12x1-2 cm, thickening towards the base, the end bulbously thickened, sheathed in an adnate rough volva of which only the upper edge is free; the stem surface white, yellowish, with a drooping ring. Flesh white, soft, smelling of rotten potatoes, with an unpleasant taste. Characteristic features: cap, gills and stem yellowish, with an unpleasant smell of rotten potatoes. Grows singly or in groups. Poisonous. Very common. Fairly often the white variety of the false death cap (Amnita citrina var. alba (Gilb.) Gilb.) is found – photo in the right-hand corner. Poisonous.

geltonasis-baltikas.features: Grows under oaks, hazels, birches, more slender than the yellow knight
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 3-5 (8) cm across, finely fibrous, greenish-yellow, sulphur-yellow, with a violet tinge in the centre. Gills sulphur-yellow, adnate. Stem 5-10x0.5-1.5 cm, the colour of the cap. Flesh not fleshy, firm, greenish-yellow, with a pungent smell of gas and an unpleasant taste. Characteristic features: a greenish-yellow fungus, flesh yellow, with an unpleasant smell and taste. Grows singly. Poisonous. Common. Similar to the yellow knight, but grows in deciduous forests and, unlike it, smells unpleasant and is not tasty. It may also occur in coniferous forests, under birches.

hornemano-gleiviabude.features: Stem with a ring, flaky-fibrous or flocculose
desc: Fruiting bodies large. Cap grows up to 15 cm across, fleshy, sticky in wet weather, yellowish-grey, greyish-brown, with a violet tinge. Young gills grey, old ones violet-blackish-brown, adnate. Stem 5-15x1-3 cm, cylindrical, white, with a broad, conspicuous ring, not thickened at the base, with white mycelial threads. Flesh whitish, thick, soft, with an unpleasant smell and taste. Characteristic features: the largest Stropharia, cap surface smooth, greyish-brown, with a violet tinge. Grows in small groups, favouring humus-rich soil; attractive-looking fungi, but mildly poisonous. Not rare.

kilnioji-musmire.habitat: Coniferous forests with an admixture of oak
kilnioji-musmire.features: Cap yellowish-bronze, with yellow scales, spores non-amyloid
desc: Cap 8-12 (15) cm across, sticky in wet weather, yellowish-brown, yellowish-bronze, the central part especially covered with yellow, greyish-yellow patches of the veil, like rough scales or warts, the margin smooth or slightly furrowed. Gills white, with a yellowish tinge, broad, free. Stem 8-15 (25)x1-2.5 cm, white, yellowish, with a white ring that is yellowish on the underside and has yellow edges, at the base with a yellowish, as if rough, adnate volva. Flesh thick, soft, white, with an unpleasant smell. Characteristic features: very similar to the fly agaric, differing in its greenish-yellow colour. Grows singly or in small groups in mature coniferous forests with an admixture of oak and birch. Poisonous, like the fly agaric – an adornment of the forest. Protected. Rare.

Fruiting bodies small. Cap 3–5 cm across, bell-shaped, later flattened, with an inconspicuous umbo, faintly scaly, carmine, blood-red, the margin paler. Gills notched, blood-red, brownish-red, notched. Stem 3-9x0.3-0.8 cm, of a slightly paler colour than the cap. Flesh thin, red, with an unpleasant smell, slightly bitter-tasting.
Characteristic features: fruiting bodies small, not fleshy, growing mostly only in coniferous forests.

kugine-guotene.habitat: Forest edges, roadsides, damp, grassy, open places
kugine-guotene.features: Cap and stem turn black with age and as they dry
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 2-6 cm across, sometimes larger, conical, orange-red, reddish-yellow, sometimes fading to yellow, greenish-yellow. Gills adnate, broad, yellowish. Stem 5-10x0.5-1.5 cm, of even thickness, twisted, fibrous, greenish-yellow, when old blackish-spotted or entirely black. Flesh yellowish, turning black when cut or broken, without any particular smell, mild-tasting. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies orange-red, greenish-yellow, blackening. Grows in sunlit places among grass, singly or in small groups. Mildly poisonous. Common.

margoji-musmire.habitat: Deciduous, coniferous and mixed forests, parks
margoji-musmire.features: Cap with white scales, volva rough, fused with the stem
desc: Fruiting bodies large. Cap 5-10 (12) cm across, hemispherical, finally flattened, pale brown, greyish-brown, yellowish-brown, the surface covered with small white scales and warts. Gills white, crowded, broad, free. Stem 7-12x1-2 cm, white, fibrous, as if flocculose, with a ring, slightly thickening downwards, the base bulbously thickened, sheathed in a firmly attached white, as if rough volva, above which stretch 1-3 more delicate, fibrous ring-like fragments. Flesh white, with an unpleasant smell. Characteristic features: a clearly amanita-like appearance, rather repellent. Grows singly or in small groups. Poisonous. Common.

melsvazale-gleiviabude.features: Fruiting bodies slimy, greenish-blue, with white fibrous scales
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 3-7 (10) cm across, slimy, scaly, bluish-green. Gills violet-brown, chocolate-coloured when old. Stem 4-10x0.3-2 cm, with a ring, the colour of the cap, fibrous-scaly. Flesh whitish, with an unpleasant smell and taste. Characteristic features: appears on rotten wood and decayed plant debris, in small groups. Grows on rotten wood, humus-rich soil and other rotten organic matter, several fruiting bodies together. Inedible or even mildly poisonous; some authors write that it is edible. Common.

melynoji-gijabude.features: Cap blackish-blue, stem bluish above, white below
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 3-6 cm across, conical at first, later flattened with a conspicuous blunt umbo, the margin bent downwards, finely fibrillose, greyish-blue, the central part blackish-blue, fading. Young gills white, later pink, brownish-pink, adnexed. Stem 3-7 (10)x0.2-0.7 cm, thickened in the middle, tapering towards the base, the colour of the cap, whitish at the base. Flesh thin, white, bluish under the cuticle, with a faint smell of flour. Characteristic features: stem tapering, spores almost round. Grows singly in old mixed spruce forests, in grassy places, favouring acidic soil. Very rare, should be classed as protected.

muilinis-baltikas.features: Cap with a smooth surface, fleshy
desc: Fruiting bodies medium to large. Cap 7–10 (12) cm across, fleshy, greyish-metallic, greenish, violet-blackish or even pale brownish-yellowish. Gills white, old ones greenish-yellowish, pink-spotted, adnate. Stem 5-10x0.5-3 cm, whitish, greyish-brownish when old. Flesh thick, white, pinkish when older, turning even more distinctly pink when broken or cut, with an unpleasant smell and a soapy taste. Characteristic features: cap usually pink-spotted, especially when old. Grows singly or in small groups, favouring mossy places. Some sources state that it is inedible or even mildly poisonous, others that it is edible but of little value. Mildly poisonous (causes brief stomach pains, vomiting, nausea). Not rare.

Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 3-6 (8) cm across, conical, later flattened with a blunt umbo, orange-brown, reddish-brown, finely fibrous or even scaly. Gills thick, distant, reddish-brown, cinnamon-brown, adnate. Stem 3–9x0.5- 1.5 cm, tapering at the base, yellowish-brown, reddish-brown fibrous. Flesh yellowish, with an unpleasant smell, mild-tasting. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies reddish-orange, spores large. Grows singly or in small groups under oaks and birches, rarely also occurring in pine forests. Deadly poisonous. The poisonous substances are orellanine and other polypeptides.

nuodingoji-tauriabude.habitat: Forest clearings, forest edges, meadows, parks
nuodingoji-tauriabude.features: Fruiting bodies white, grey, old ones even brownish
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 2-4 (6) cm across, matt, white, greyish, brownish, with a white bloom. Gills whitish, narrow. Stem 3-5x0.3-0.7 cm, white, brownish when old. Flesh thin, whitish, smelling of stale flour and gas. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies smell of stale flour, grow in thickets and grassy places. Appears as several fruiting bodies together or in small groups among grass. Poisonous. Common. In all, 112 species of Clitocybe have been described, in Lithuania so far 41. Some species are edible but of little value, several are poisonous, among them this one, which contains muscarine and alkaloids.

paprastoji-ankstene.habitat: Coniferous and deciduous forests, parks, even gardens, pastures, fallow land
paprastoji-ankstene.features: Fruiting bodies round, skin hard, warty, gleba black when mature
desc: Fruiting bodies large, almost globose, 5-12 cm across, the skin thick, cracked, warty, scaly. Young ones lemon-coloured, old ones ochre, brownish-yellow. There is no stem. Young flesh white, pink when cut, old flesh violet-black, almost black, interlaced with white threads, with an unpleasant smell. Characteristic features: firmly attached to the substrate by a tuft of rhizoids. The flesh, unlike that of puffballs, is bluish-black. Grows in forests, parks and forest edges, often on forest roadsides and slopes, singly or in small groups. Favours sandy, humus-rich soil. Not rare. Poisonous.

paprastoji-musmire.habitat: Deciduous, coniferous and mixed forests, parks
paprastoji-musmire.features: Cap bright red, with white scales and spots
desc: Fruiting bodies large. Cap grows up to 25 cm across, bright red, orange-red, with irregularly shaped patches or warts of the white veil. Gills broad, crowded, white, yellowish when old. Stem 8-22x2-3 cm, white, with a ring, the base bulbously thickened, fused with the volva, looking as if ragged. Flesh white, orange under the cuticle, soft, thick, without any particular smell or taste. Characteristic features: stem without a volva, only with flaky remnants, spores non-amyloid. Grows singly, mostly in larger or smaller groups. Poisonous, very common. An adornment of the forest. Poisonous substances identified: muscarine, muscaridine, muscimol, bufotenine, ibotenic acid (some of them have hallucinogenic properties).

pilkalakste-plausabude.features: Grows only on bare, humus-rich, damp soil
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 0.5-2 (3-4) cm across, conical when young, later flattened, with a sharp umbo, white, greyish-white, grey or even cream. Young gills white, later greyish-brown, adnate. Stem 3–7x0.1-0.4 cm, white, fragile. Flesh white, thin, with an unpleasant smell and taste. Characteristic features: tiny, white fruiting bodies that do not catch the mushroom picker's eye. Grows singly or in small groups. Poisonous, very common. There are several varieties, differing only in their blue or pink colour, growing next to one another.

pilkoji-meskute.habitat: Coniferous, deciduous and mixed forests, bogs, parks, gardens
pilkoji-meskute.features: Yellowish-greenish-brown fruiting bodies, turning brown when pressed or cut
desc: Medium-sized, rarely large fungi. Cap grows up to 12 cm across, more rarely larger, matt, velvety, yellowish-greenish-brownish. Gills yellowish, greenish-yellowish, old ones dirty brown. Stem 4-8x1-2 cm, slightly paler than the cap. Flesh yellowish, later brownish-brown, turning brown when broken or cut. Characteristic features: tough, soft, attractive-looking fungi. Grows in larger or smaller groups, very common. It used to be considered edible, but over the last two or three decades it has been recognised as poisonous in many European countries; it has been found to contain lead, muscarine and strontium, which are harmful to human health. Well boiled it is less poisonous, but it is suitable neither for salting nor for pickling, so this fungus should not be abused.

puokstine-kelmabude.habitat: On stumps, snags and windfalls of coniferous and deciduous trees
puokstine-kelmabude.features: Young gills and upper part of the stem sulphur-yellow
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 3–5 cm across, growing even larger, sulphur-yellow, pale yellow, yellowish-brown in the middle, when old yellowish-greenish-brown, not fleshy. Young gills the colour of sulphur powder, old ones greenish-blackish-brown. Stem up to 10 cm long and up to 1 cm thick, the upper part sulphur-yellow, lower down the stem yellowish-brownish; not far from the cap there is a dark greyish-greenish ring-like remnant of the partial veil. Flesh yellow, bitter, with an unpleasant smell. Characteristic features: young fruiting bodies sulphur-yellow. Grows in groups, sometimes in large colonies. Poisonous. Very common. It has attracted the interest of physicians. It does not resemble honey fungi; when mature it has greenish-blackish-brown gills.

raudonlakstis-nuosedis.features: Very similar to the cinnamon webcap, with brownish-orange gills
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 3-5 cm across, rarely larger, conical when young, finally becoming raised-flattened, with an umbo, surface smooth or finely fibrous, when dried even scaly, greenish-yellowish-brown, reddish-brown. Gills blood-red, old ones brownish-red, adnate. Stem 3-10x0.3-1 cm, pale ochre-yellow, the lower part yellowish-pink. Flesh thin, yellowish-brown, smelling of iodoform and radish, slightly bitter. Characteristic features: blood-red gills, cap and stem yellowish, ochre-brown. Grows in small groups, mostly in coniferous and mixed forests. Poisonous, common.

raudonzvynis-nuosedis.features: Gills yellow, orange, reddish-brown when mature
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 3-6 cm across, rarely larger, convex, flattened, creamy yellow when young, later reddish-brown, pinkish-brown, covered with yellowish-red scales, veil rusty-red. Gills pale yellow, later reddish-brown, adnate, semi-decurrent. Stem 3-9x0.3-1.3 cm, white when young, soon becoming the colour of the cap, finely scaly. Flesh white, becoming chrome-yellow when cut or broken. Characteristic features: cap and stem with reddish-brown scales, flesh turns yellow when cut. Grows singly or in small groups, favouring the vicinity of birch, aspen and oak. Poisonous.

Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 3-8 cm across, rarely larger, conical, finally raised-flattened, with a sharp umbo, orange-red, reddish-brown, fibrous-scaly, rough, the margin bent downwards. Gills thick, distant, the colour of the cap, broad, adnate. Stem 7–9x1-1.3 cm, of even thickness, tapering at the base, the colour of the cap, fibrous-scaly. Flesh orange-yellow, with an unpleasant smell of radish and an unpleasant taste. Characteristic features: cap and stem orange-brown, with an unpleasant smell. Grows in small groups, favouring damp, grassy places in old spruce forests. Deadly poisonous. Rare, found only in the Dubrava forests (Kaunas district).

rausvavarude-musmire.features: Cap and stem greyish-brown, volva fused with the stem
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 5-9 cm across, greyish-violet, greyish-brown, with a smooth surface, shiny. Gills white, crowded. Stem 5–10x0.5–1.5 cm, grey, greyish-brown, with a delicate falling-off ring, bulbously thickened at the base, with a white, greyish-brownish-violet adnate volva. Flesh thin, soft, with an unpleasant smell of rotten potatoes. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies do not resemble amanitas, smaller than those of other amanitas, the cap cuticle elastic, tough, peeling easily. Grows singly, sometimes several fruiting bodies together. Mildly poisonous. Common.

rausvejancioji-plausabude.features: Fruiting bodies whitish, cream, darkening and turning pinkish when old
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 3–9 cm, conical, bell-shaped, fibrous, whitish when young, later yellowish, yellowish-orange, red-spotted. Gills white, later greyish-brown. Stem 3-8 (10)x0.5-1.5 cm, thickening towards the base, white, without a ring. Flesh white, soft, with an unpleasant smell and taste. Characteristic features: cap, gills, stem and flesh turn red when pressed or broken. Grows in spring, favouring calcareous soil. Not rare. A deadly poisonous fungus, containing 20 times more muscarine than the fly agaric. Similar to the field and edible (horse) mushrooms, but these do not turn red and their gills are chocolate-coloured and the stem has a ring; also similar to St George's mushroom, but that does not turn red when pressed or cut.

rozine-salmabude.habitat: Forests, parks, grassy, damp places, on the ground and forest litter
desc: Fruiting bodies, as is typical of the genus Mycena, small. Cap 3–6 cm across, conical when young, later flattened, with an umbo, hygrophanous, greyish-pink, pale pink, fading to cream or even whitish, the margin translucently furrowed. Gills distant, broad, white, pale pink when mature, adnexed. Stem 3-8 (10)x0.3-1 cm, thickening towards the base, brownish or the colour of the cap, white-hairy and bristly at the base. Flesh thin, white, smelling of radish and gas. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies fading, with an unpleasant smell of radish and gas. Grows singly or in small groups. Poisonous, containing muscarine. Very common.
