The symptoms of poisoning are very similar to those caused by the stinking bonnet, whose fruiting bodies are violet, pinkish-violet and grow in the same places. Common.

rudenine-kugiabude.habitat: Forests, parks, rotten deciduous and coniferous wood
rudenine-kugiabude.features: Stem with a ring, conspicuously white-fibrous, which is not characteristic of the funeral bell
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 2-6 cm across, hemispherical, later convex, finally flattened or slightly raised, sticky when wet, orange-brown, pale ochre when dry, the margin not furrowed. Young gills cream, later ochre, brown, broad, distant, broadly adnate, semi-decurrent, edges white-notched. Stem 2-6 (9)x0.3-0.7 cm, of even thickness, most often thickening towards the base, ochre-brown, with a fibrous, sometimes membranous ring, white-dotted above it. Flesh cream, mild-tasting, smelling of flour. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies orange-brown, growing in autumn. Appears singly or in small groups in forests, parks and open places. Uncommon. Deadly poisonous.

rudeninis-bobausis.features: Grows only in autumn, cap mitre-shaped
desc: Fruiting bodies large. Cap 5-10 (15) cm across, usually with two or four lobes, mitre-shaped, brown, chestnut-coloured, rather fragile. Stem 3-12x1-3 cm, thickening towards the base, smooth, sometimes slightly wrinkled lengthwise, whitish, pale yellowish-brown. Flesh whitish, with a pleasant smell and taste. Characteristic features: cap lobed but not curly-wrinkled, stem whitish. Grows singly or in small groups, on decayed wood or humus-rich soil. Edible when dried and well boiled. Poisonous when fresh.

samaninis-piengrybis.habitat: Damp coniferous forests, especially swampy sphagnum pine forests
desc: Fruiting bodies rather stout. Cap 6-10 (15) cm across, fleshy, fibrous, velvety, matt, pinkish-ochre, orange-grey, sometimes with a faint violet tinge; gills cream, yellowish. Stem 5-12x1-3 (4) cm, the colour of the cap. Flesh yellowish, pale brownish-ochre, firm, brittle, not bitter, when dried with a strong smell of coumarin, the juice clear, colourless. Spores finely warty, the spore mass white or yellowish. A characteristic feature of these fungi is the milky juice, usually white. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies yellowish, the milky juice scanty, watery, colourless. In Lithuania 54 species of Lactarius have been found. Grows singly or in small groups. The fenugreek milkcap is inedible, even mildly poisonous.

setoninis-baravykas.habitat: Deciduous forests, especially calcareous oak woods with limes and hazels
setoninis-baravykas.features: Stem bulbously swollen downwards, with a red net
desc: Fruiting bodies stout, fleshy. Cap grows up to 30 cm across and the stem up to 10 cm thick. Cap surface matt, pale grey, without a pinkish or rosy tinge, darkening when pressed – becoming greenish-grey. Tubes yellowish, up to 3 cm long, and the pores soft red, carmine-red, greenish-bluish when pressed. Stem very thick, almost round when young, leathery-yellow near the tubes, carmine-red lower down, adorned with a net of the same red. Flesh pale, almost white, turning slightly blue when broken or cut, with a nutty taste and a specific smell. Characteristic features: cap grey, flesh turns slightly blue. Grows in small groups or singly. Inedible, mildly poisonous. Found in the vicinity of Vilnius.

sieralakstis-nuosedis.habitat: Coniferous and deciduous forests, especially dry pine forests
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 1.5–6 cm across, conical, finally becoming flattened, with an umbo, matt, fibrous, finely scaly, dark brownish-red, then becoming greenish-brownish-yellow, yellowish-brown, the margin paler, the veil pale yellow. Young gills sulphur-yellow, later yellowish-brown, adnate. Stem 3–7 (10-12)x0.3-1 cm, yellow, later reddish-brown, whitish at the base, with an inconspicuous ring-like remnant of the veil. Flesh yellow, thin, smelling of radish, with an unpleasant taste, slightly bitter. Characteristic features: cap greenish-brownish-yellow, fibrous, stem of similar colour. Grows singly or in small groups in forests, especially in dry pine forests, mostly in autumn. Not rare. Poisonous.

siurpioji-plausabude.habitat: Forests, parks, sandy shrublands, willow thickets
siurpioji-plausabude.features: A fungus of damp, grassy places, spores very large
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 2-4 cm across, bell-shaped-convex when young, later raised-flattened, with a blunt umbo, shaggy, fibrous-scaly on a brown background. Gills pale brown, later umber-brown, reddish-brown, adnexed. Stem 3-5x0.2-0.5 cm, of even thickness, brown. Flesh thin, yellowish, brownish, with an unpleasant smell, not bitter. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies umber-brown, cap roughly scaly. Grows in small groups, mostly in coniferous, deciduous and mixed forests, in damp grassy places. Poisonous, very common. An untempting, unattractive fungus.

smailiakepure-musmire.habitat: Coniferous forests, mature spruce forests, pine forests with an admixture of spruce
smailiakepure-musmire.features: Cap white, conical, not scaly, stem with a non-adnate volva
desc: Fruiting bodies large. Cap grows up to 10 cm across, acutely conical, flattened when old but with a conspicuous, pointed umbo, white, matt, surface smooth. Gills white, free. Stem 8-17x1–2 cm, white, thickening downwards, with an inconspicuous, sometimes ragged, falling-off ring, the base enclosed in a large, loose, non-adnate white volva. Flesh thick, white, smelling of rotten potatoes and stale radishes. Characteristic features: spores round, amyloid, the fungus turns yellow with KOH solution. Grows mostly singly, among mosses, in old-growth forests. Deadly poisonous; 6 poisonous substances (polypeptides) have been isolated. In toxicity it is not inferior to the death cap.

smailiazvyne-zvynabudele.habitat: Forest edges, parks, gardens, cemeteries, shady, grassy places
desc: Fruiting bodies large. Cap 8-15 cm across, covered on a yellowish background with pointed, sharp, brownish-brown scales that rub off. Gills white, very crowded, up to 1 cm wide. Stem 5-10x1-2 cm, with a ring, above it white, smooth, below yellowish-brown, fibrous-scaly. Flesh white, soft, with a pleasant smell and taste, up to 1 cm thick, not bitter. Characteristic features: beautiful scaly fruiting bodies growing among grass, reminiscent of a little partridge or even a hedgehog. In some places it is confused with the parasol mushroom, but there is no resemblance whatsoever between them. Grows singly or several or even a dozen or so fruiting bodies together, most often in parks, favouring humus-rich soil. Inedible, slightly poisonous.

Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 3–7 (10) cm across, conical when young, finally shaped like an open umbrella, with a sharp umbo, the cuticle radially cracked, often split, from yellowish to brownish-red. Gills greyish, later yellowish-brown, adnexed. Stem 3-8 (13)x0.3-7.5 cm, yellowish-brownish, whitish near the gills, white-dotted. Flesh white, yellowish, with an unpleasant smell and taste. Characteristic features: cap conical, cracked, stem thin, long. Grows singly or in small groups. Poisonous, common. A fungus of repellent appearance. In Lithuania 65 species of Inocybe have been found so far. Most are mycosymbiotrophs. Every second or third species is poisonous, the others are inedible. These fungi are of no interest to mushroom pickers.

valgomasis-bobausis.habitat: Coniferous and mixed forests, especially pine forests
desc: Fruiting bodies massive. Cap 5-15 cm across, shapeless, convolutedly wrinkled, hollow, light or dark brown, chestnut-coloured, sometimes yellowish. Stem (3–8x2–3 cm) short, thick, white, yellowish, greyish, brown when old. Flesh fragile, with a pleasant smell and taste. Characteristic features: grows only in pine and spruce forests, in April–May. Appears singly or in groups, sometimes quite abundantly, favouring bright places – clearings, roadsides, felling sites, burnt areas. Common. Conditionally poisonous, although it is still gathered and eaten. There is no consensus about its use as food; for example, in Canada and Finland it is eaten without restriction, and dried ones are even bought up from Lithuania. Nevertheless, it should not be eaten.

varpelinis-meslinukas.habitat: Forests, parks, pastures, fallow land, meadows
varpelinis-meslinukas.features: Cap bell- or helmet-shaped, stem brownish, white-dotted
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 1–3 cm across, rarely larger, bell-shaped, greyish-brown, grey, smooth, dry, the margin white-toothed. Gills dark grey, finally greyish-black, the edges white-„encrusted“. Stem 7-12x0.2-0.3 cm, slender, brownish, with a bloom. Flesh brownish, thin, without any particular smell or taste. Characteristic features: cap greyish-brown, stem thin, long, spores lemon-shaped, black. Grows on the excrement of wild animals, in small groups. Very common. Has psychotropic, hallucinogenic properties; of interest to physicians.

stambioji-gijabude.features: The largest fungus of the genus Entoloma, fruiting bodies flesh-coloured
desc: Fruiting bodies large, massive. Cap grows up to 15 cm across and considerably larger, of irregular shape, the margin sometimes cracked, greyish-brownish, creamy-brownish, flesh-coloured. Young gills yellowish, later ochre-pink, reddish-brown, broad, thick, adnate. Stem 5-12 (15-20)x0.5-3 (4) cm, whitish. Flesh with a pungent smell of flour and an unpleasant taste. Characteristic features: flesh smelling of flour, with a sharp taste; grows more in autumn than in summer, in forests, rarely in parks. Grows singly or in small groups, favouring clayey soil and the vicinity of birch and oak. Poisonous, uncommon, dangerous. Sometimes it occurs even in gardens.

svelnusis-skiautenelis.habitat: On fallen pine branches, windfalls, stumps
svelnusis-skiautenelis.features: Fruiting bodies tough, hardy, unafraid of frost
desc: Fruiting bodies tiny. Cap 0.5-2 (3) cm across, round, kidney-shaped, flattened, greyish, brownish, very tough. Gills elastic, white when young, later brownish, leathery, narrow, adnexed. Stem 0.2-0.8x0.2-0.5 cm, lateral, tapering, white, fibrous. Flesh tough, white, thin, with an unpleasant taste, without any particular smell. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies yellowish-brownish, stem lateral, grows only on dead coniferous, especially pine, wood. Appears in small groups or groups. An active wood saprotroph. Very common, alive during thaws and in winter. There are reports that it is poisonous.

zalsvoji-guotene.habitat: Open places: meadows, pastures, roadsides, forests
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 1.5-3 (5) cm across, bell-shaped, soon becoming flattened, with an umbo, slimy, green when young, greenish-yellow, orange-yellow with greenish spots when mature. Gills the colour of the cap, adnate. Stem 3-8x0.3-0.8 cm, slimy when young, the colour of the cap. Flesh thin, not fleshy, the colour of the cap, without any particular smell or taste. Characteristic features: cap, gills, stem and flesh green, in mature fungi greenish-yellow. Grows in summer and autumn in small groups, in sunlit places, among grass (in meadows, forest edges, fallow land). Poisonous.

Fruiting bodies small. Cap 2-3 (6) cm across, irregularly flattened, with an inconspicuous umbo, sometimes barely depressed, fibrous or even scaly, yellowish-brown, greenish-brownish-yellow. Gills pale greyish-yellow, later greenish-brown, notched. Stem 3-7x0.3-0.8 cm, whitish, yellowish, brown when old, sometimes with a ring-like remnant of the veil. Flesh thin, yellowish-brownish, bitter-tasting. Characteristic features: greenish-yellowish-brownish fruiting bodies, growing in groups. Appears in coniferous and deciduous forests, favouring sandy, stony soil. Poisonous, very common. Similar to the sour woodtuft, but that one grows only on wood.

zalsvoji-musmire.habitat: Forests, parks, favours the vicinity of oak and birch
zalsvoji-musmire.features: Cap green, greyish- or yellowish-green, volva not fused with the stem
desc: Fruiting bodies large. Cap 6–12 (15) cm across, enclosed in a white veil when young, later flattened, usually with adhering bits of the white veil. Gills white, crowded, broad. Stem 5-15x1-2.5 cm, white, greyish, often with a yellowish-greenish tinge and with transverse oblique greenish bands, a white ring, and at the base a large, white, loose volva whose edge sometimes protrudes above the ground. Flesh white, thick, mild-tasting, with an unpleasant smell of rotting potatoes. Characteristic features: cap green, spores amyloid. Grows singly or in groups, more common in deciduous forests. A deadly poisonous fungus in which 16 poisonous substances have been identified.

zieduotasis-baltikas.features: Stem with a ring, spores small, round
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized, rarely large. Cap 5-12 cm across, convex when young, later flattened with an inconspicuous blunt umbo, orange-brown, yellowish-brown, the margin paler. Gills white, later yellowish, adnate or free. Stem 6-8x1.5-2 cm, tapering towards the base, with a ring, below it orange-brown flaky. Flesh white, firm, thick, with an unpleasant smell and taste. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies orange-brown, chestnut-coloured. Grows singly or several together in pine forests, in more open sandy places, more common in the forests of south-eastern Lithuania. Inedible; some sources even list it as poisonous. Uncommon.

degesine-trapiabude.features: Young fungi look as if snowed upon, frosted, with white flakes
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 1.5-4 cm across, at first conical, bell-shaped, flocculose-fibrous, later raised-flattened, dirty greyish-brown, fading to greyish-yellowish, white-fibrous. Gills greyish, old ones purplish-brown, edges whitish. Stem 2-5 (7)x0.2–0.5 cm, white, white-fibrous. Flesh whitish, without smell or taste. Characteristic features: cap greyish-brown, stem white, conspicuously white-fibrous, as if shaggy. Grows from spring to autumn on burnt areas and bonfire sites, among grass, singly or in small groups. A carbotroph; it would be suitable for neutralising (breaking down) charred wood on burnt sites.

Fruiting bodies tiny, small. Cap 0.5–1.5 cm across, conical at first, later convex-flattened, flattened, with a sharp umbo, surface smooth, becoming rough and even finely scaly when dried, the margin furrowed or smooth, dark brownish-red, chestnut-coloured, fading in dry weather to brownish-yellowish. Gills ochre-brown, adnate. Stem 1.5-4x0.1-0.3 cm, of even thickness, hollow, from pale to dark reddish-brown, white-fibrous. Flesh yellowish, brown, thin, slightly bitter-tasting. Characteristic features: tiny fungi, cap with a pointed, sharp umbo. Grows mostly in autumn, singly or in small groups among grass, under beeches. Otherwise rare, although in the Dubrava forests (Kaunas district) it is often found under beeches.

gelsvasis-klumpiaausis.habitat: On rotten deciduous wood, herbaceous plant debris
gelsvasis-klumpiaausis.features: Without a stem or with only traces of one
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 1-3 cm across, roundly kidney-shaped when young, later irregularly fan-shaped, the margin wavy; fragile, at first white, silky-fibrous, white, yellowish; with age the fibrils disappear. Gills crowded, white, cream, old ones ochre-brownish, brown. Stem only rudimentary or entirely absent, the cap attached to the substrate by its side or back. Flesh thin. Characteristic features: cap white, yellowish, fibrous. Grows in small groups in forests, parks and gardens on rotten deciduous wood. Uncommon. Saprotroph.

Fruiting bodies small. Cap 1.5-3 (4) cm across, ovoid-cylindrical when young, later bell-shaped, white-fibrous, finally shaped like an open umbrella, grey, the margin grooved. Gills white, soon becoming grey, then black. Stem 7-15x0.3-0.8 cm, thickening towards the base, white-woolly, hairy, fibrous, smooth when old. Flesh thin, whitish, odourless. Characteristic features: the fungus is fragile, cap grey, white-fibrous, as if scurfy. Grows singly, among grass, on rotten wood. Common. 85 species of Coprinus have been described, 31 found in Lithuania, all saprotrophs; some have antibiotic medicinal properties, they are a good subject of laboratory research, and physicians take an interest in them.

konrado-guotene.habitat: Open, grassy places, forest edges, parks, roadsides
konrado-guotene.features: Cap and stem orange-yellow, gills yellow
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 3-7 cm across, bluntly conical, surface smooth, sticky, orange-yellow, fading when old to greyish-brownish. Gills yellow, edges paler, thick, distant, adnate. Stem 6–7x0.3–1 cm, of even thickness, yellowish-orange, paler at the base. Flesh thin, yellow, the stem flesh white, not blackening when cut, without any particular smell or taste. Characteristic features: spores large, broadly elliptical. Grows singly or several fruiting bodies together in forests and on forest edges – in open, grassy places. Food value unknown. Rare.

lipnioji-skujagalve.habitat: Trunks, snags and stumps of deciduous trees
lipnioji-skujagalve.features: Cap and stem scaly, very slimy
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized, rarely large. Cap 5–8 (10-15) cm across, flattened when mature, with or without a blunt umbo, slimy, yellowish-brown, scaly. Gills pale yellow, old ones greenish-brownish-brown, crowded, adnate. Stem 5–8 (10)x0.5-1.5 cm, thickening towards the base, slimy, scaly. Flesh yellowish-brown, soft, not bitter, without any particular smell. Characteristic features: very similar to the golden scalycap, but the latter's fruiting bodies are not slimy and its spores are larger (8-10x5-6 pm). Grows singly or in small groups, in summer and autumn, on deciduous trees, most often on aspen and black alder stumps, trunks and snags. Food value unknown. Rarer than the golden scalycap.

Fruiting bodies small. Cap 3-5 cm across, bell-shaped when young, later conically bell-shaped, pleated-lobed, reddish-brown, yellowish-brown, with glittering particles, when old becoming brownish-grey, the margin blackish. Gills whitish, old ones black. Stem 3-8 (10)x0.3–0.5 cm, whitish, brownish when old. Flesh thin, white, brownish, without any particular smell or taste. Characteristic features: very similar to the glistening inkcap, but grows in much smaller groups or even singly. Grows in summer and autumn on rotten wood lying on the ground and on the soil surface. Rare, a wood saprotroph. Food value unknown.

melsvoji-gleiviabude.habitat: Grassy forests, forest edges, parks, thickets
melsvoji-gleiviabude.features: Fruiting bodies blue, spores larger than those of the verdigris roundhead
desc: Fruiting bodies small to medium-sized. Cap 3-5 (8) cm across, raised-flattened, flattened, with a blunt umbo, blue, fading to greyish-bluish-greenish, white-scaly. Gills grey, soon violet-brown, adnexed. Stem 3-7 (10)x0.5–1.8 cm, with a fragmentary ring, above which it is bluish, white-fibrillose, below greyish-bluish, white-flocculose or fibrous, as if bristling. Flesh bluish, later whitish, with a mushroomy smell, not bitter.
Characteristic features: the similar pale roundhead (S. pseudocyanea) grows in the same places, but its fruiting bodies are only bluish-greenish, faintly fibrous, finely scaly.
Appears singly or in small groups in gloomy, grassy, damp places. Food value unknown.

pelkinis-piengrybis.features: Milk white, turning yellow on contact with air
desc: Medium-sized fruiting bodies. Cap 3-6 cm across, convex when young, soon raised-flattened, flattened, with or without an umbo, slightly depressed, surface unzoned, orange-brown, yellowish-orange, brick-red. Gills whitish, the colour of the cap; the stem hollow when old. Flesh thin, slightly acrid-tasting, with white milk that turns yellow on contact with air. Characteristic features: very similar to the mild milkcap (L. mitissimus) and the pale milkcap (L. thejogalus), but the bog milkcap prefers the vicinity of birch and grassy places. Grows singly or in groups in mixed or purely deciduous forests. Food value unknown. Common, abundant in places.

pievine-meslinuke.habitat: Meadows, pastures, squares, among grass, lawns
desc: Fruiting bodies tiny. Cap 0.5-1.5 (2.5) cm, bell-shaped when young, later flattened-conical, flattened, with an umbo, fading, smooth, dry, greyish-brown, yellowish-greyish-brown, sand-coloured. Gills pale greyish-brown, brown, chocolate, adnate. Stem 3-7x0.1-0.3 cm, of even thickness, hollow, cream, greyish-brownish. Flesh thin, brownish, not bitter. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies fragile, gills brown, chocolate-coloured. Grows in summer and autumn, singly, in meadows, pastures and lawns. A nitrophile. Very common. Has psychotropic properties and ought to interest physicians as well

pleiskanotasis-meslagrybis.features: Similar to the glistening inkcap, cap blunt, with a layer of “powder”
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 3-5 cm across, bluntly conical, sand-coloured, yellowish-brown, white-scurfy, fibrous, furrowed, pleated. Gills whitish, cream, old ones blackish-brown. Stem 5-7 (8)x0.3–0.5 cm, white, cream, with a white bloom. Flesh thin, fragile, yellowish, without any particular smell or taste. Characteristic features: cap yellowish-brown, white-“powdered”, spores almost round. Grows on old stumps and windfalls, in tufts. Rare. A wood saprotroph, food value unknown. The glistening inkcap and this inkcap are easily confused, especially at the mature, old stage.

rausvejantis-balsvis.habitat: Roadsides, areas near houses, parks, squares
rausvejantis-balsvis.features: Fruiting bodies white, turning greyish and brownish as they grow or when touched
desc: Fruiting bodies large. Cap 5-10 (15) cm across, flattened, greyish-white, greyish-brownish when old, fibrous, scaly, turning brownish when pressed, soon fading, the margin with remnants of the veil. Gills whitish, later cream, old ones with a soft brownish-pink tinge, free. Stem 6-10x1-2.5 cm, white, with a ring, darkening with age, turning brownish when pressed. Flesh white, yellowish, turning brownish when pressed, not bitter. Characteristic features: gills whitish, cream, brownish when mature. Grows singly or in small groups, favouring rich, humus-rich soil. Rare. Food value unknown.

spindulinis-rauksliagrybis.habitat: On rotten coniferous and deciduous wood
desc: Fruiting bodies spreading, of waxy consistency, soft, hardening with age, from pale pinkish to violet-red. Hymenophore wrinkled, in the form of radially arranged folds, paler and fibrous at the margins. Characteristic features: a round fruiting body of waxy consistency, ochre-pink, spreading radially. Grows in forests and parks on windfalls, more rarely on snags and stumps, in autumn, in mild winters and in spring. Causes a white rot of the wood. A fairly common wood destroyer. Saprotroph.

stambioji-kiskiabude.features: The largest Conocybe, fruiting bodies sand-coloured, spores small
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 3-7 cm across, fleshy, hemispherical when young, later convex-flattened, surface smooth, sometimes slightly wrinkled, yellowish, sand-coloured, the margin grooved, usually soiled with earth, dirty. Gills cream, later yellowish-brown, broad, up to 0.7 cm wide, adnexed. Stem 2-3 (4)x0.5-2 cm thick, solid or with an inconspicuous cavity, finely fibrillose, yellowish, cream, soiled with earth in the lower part because it is deeply embedded in the soil. Flesh white, thick, up to 0.7 cm thick, not bitter, without any particular smell. Characteristic features: a fleshy, massive Conocybe. Food value unknown. Saprotroph. Grows in greenhouses and fields, in rich soil, singly or in small groups, in May–August. Adventive, warmth-loving. Protected.

trispalve-meskabude.features: Cap massive, convex, stem thickened, spores amyloid
desc: Fruiting bodies large, massive, fleshy. Cap 10-15 (25) cm across, hemispherical when young, later flattened, raised, fleshy, matt, fibrous, spotted greenish-yellowish, whitish-ochre, the margin rolled downwards. Gills narrow, very crowded, yellowish-greenish, adnate. Stem 8-10x1.5-4.5 cm, white-fibrous, firm, white, yellowish, sometimes bulbously thickened at the base. Flesh thick, firm, white, not bitter, with an unpleasant smell. Characteristic features: large, greenish-yellowish fruiting bodies, stem thick, growing only on calcareous soil, warmth-loving. Grows singly or several fruiting bodies together. Very rare, protected. Food value unknown; some sources state that it is edible. Found only in the forests of Verkiai Regional Park (Vilnius area).
